Materials ↗

Carbon & Alloy Steel ↗

A practical choice for drawing-defined fasteners where the required mechanical class, wear behavior and surface protection can be specified together.

SUS304 & SUS316 Stainless Steel ↗

Austenitic stainless choices for parts where corrosion exposure, surface condition and the specified fastener strength class need to be considered together.

Aluminum Alloys ↗

Lightweight metal options for custom threaded parts where the alloy, temper, engagement and surface requirements can be engineered for the application.

Copper ↗

A material family considered where electrical or thermal function is important alongside the geometry and mechanical acceptance of the custom component.

Brass ↗

Copper-zinc alloys can be useful for drawing-specific machined threaded components where machining behavior, contact conditions and the selected alloy composition fit the application.

Titanium & Titanium Alloys ↗

Titanium grades are considered where mass, corrosion exposure and required mechanical properties justify a grade-specific manufacturing and verification plan.

CCD Vision & Dimensional Inspection

Non-contact optical checks for screw length, head diameter and visible stepped profiles, combined with the gauges and tests required by the drawing.

Shoulder screws: drawing and acceptance matrix

Use this matrix to prepare a review. Values and acceptance methods are agreed for the actual part; these are specification fields, not catalog limits.

InterfaceWhat to defineVerification discussion
Locating diameterDiameter limits, mating bore and accepted final conditionCheck size with a suitable calibrated method; assess form separately when specified
Axial shoulder lengthSeating face to the shoulder transition; stack and required clearanceMeasure from the functional face; check the assembled axial condition
Shoulder-to-thread relationshipDatum axis, transition clearance and usable threadAgree geometry measurement and thread gauging separately

Common specification questions

Can the shoulder and thread have different diameters?

Yes, the shoulder and thread are specified independently. Review the transition, available mating clearance and effective thread engagement as one geometry.

Is every shoulder screw ground?

No. The final size, form and surface requirements determine the finishing route. Review the need for grinding with treatment distortion and the final acceptance condition.

Follow a complete application design

Explore a proposed assembly, the fastener choices, manufacturing review and sample validation plan. This is an illustrative design study, with no claimed customer delivery or measured performance.

Review the fixture shoulder and axial-stack concept ↗

Check the bore fit separately from the axial clearance

The shoulder-to-bore interface guides movement; the distance between the seating faces controls the axial stack. Define both in the finished condition rather than treating a thread fit as the locating fit.

  1. Shoulder and mating bore: specify the two limits, the reference axis and any functional surface requirement.
  2. Seating and transition: show the mating chamfer or counterbore so the incomplete thread or relief does not prevent seating.
  3. After finishing: identify the surfaces affected by treatment or coating and the stage at which the final fit is checked.

Read the clearance calculation below alongside these interfaces. A satisfactory axial gap does not by itself establish the bore fit or the required geometric relationship.

Calculate the shoulder clearance from both tolerance limits

For a moving plate, shoulder length must be compared with the complete stack between the seating faces. Include the washer, bushing and plate in that stack; overall screw length does not determine movement clearance.

Assume a shoulder length L of 8.20 ± 0.03 mm and a complete moving stack S of 8.00 ± 0.05 mm. The illustrative required axial clearance is 0.10–0.30 mm. Both dimensions refer to the final supplied condition.

Calculate the shoulder clearance from both tolerance limits
CalculationResult
Minimum clearance: shortest shoulder minus thickest stack8.17−8.05=0.12 mm
Maximum clearance: longest shoulder minus thinnest stack8.23−7.95=0.28 mm

The calculated 0.12–0.28 mm interval lies inside the illustrative requirement. That answers this axial-clearance question only: separately check shoulder-to-bore fit, transition clearance, thread engagement and the effect of the actual assembly and service conditions.

Use the drawing checklist to record both interfaces

How to prepare an inspection plan for custom screws ↗

Build an inspection plan one characteristic at a time. For each drawing requirement, record the acceptance condition, a suitable method, the inspection stage and coverage, and the evidence retained. The worked rows below show how to turn a shoulder-screw drawing into an inspection record.

ENGINEERING GUIDE

High-strength screw coatings and hydrogen-risk review ↗

A high-strength steel fastener needs a coating decision that considers both corrosion and hydrogen exposure throughout processing.

How is a shoulder screw different from a fully threaded bolt?

A shoulder screw has an unthreaded bearing or locating section between its head and thread. Select that shoulder for the required rotation, location or spacing function, and specify thread engagement separately. A fully threaded bolt does not provide the same smooth bearing surface.

How do I choose the shoulder length without clamping a moving part?

Review the complete axial stack, including washers and the mating seat. The shoulder must seat as intended while preserving the specified movement clearance. Show the assembly and tolerance stack on the drawing; nominal shoulder length alone cannot establish the final clearance.

Review the captive screw in both service positions

A captive screw belongs to a panel-and-retainer assembly. Check the released position as carefully as the tightened position; usable thread engagement and retained travel answer different questions.

  1. Released: the screw clears the mating thread while the chosen retaining feature keeps it with the panel.
  2. Tightened: the head seats as intended, the retainer has room to move and the required thread engagement remains available.
  3. Assembly review: provide panel thickness, retaining-hole details, retainer geometry and the installation sequence.

Design the retention system together

A reduced shank or retention feature must work with the panel and retaining component. Provide panel thickness, retaining-hole geometry, mating thread and assembly sequence. The screw profile alone cannot establish whether the installed fastener remains captive in every service position.

Check travel in both open and closed positions

Show the minimum movement needed to disengage the mating thread and the maximum movement permitted by the retainer. Review whether the driver remains accessible and whether the screw can contact nearby components. An illustrative access-panel review should include removal, panel opening and re-engagement, not only the tightened condition.

Define retention acceptance separately from thread fit

Agree the intended retention check, allowed movement and any repeated-service requirement. Thread gauging confirms a different characteristic from panel retention. Confirm the condition after coating and any pre-assembly, and keep the approved retaining arrangement identified with the screw drawing.

THE COMPLETE MANUFACTURING CHAIN

From raw stock.
To a verified requirement.

Select a forming route, define the functional operations and agree the final material, surface and inspection condition.

01 / CHOOSE THE ROOT ROUTE

Four ways to start.

Compare complete route examples ↗
ROUTE 01 / FORMING

Multi-Station Cold Heading ↗

Wire is cut and formed through a sequence of dies. Head, flange and some shoulder features can be integrated into a repeatable production route.

ROUTE 02 / BAR MACHINING

Swiss-Type & CNC Turning ↗

Bar-fed turning and turn-mill operations create drawing-specific steps, bores and other details with flexible programming.

ROUTE 03 / HEATED FORMING

Hot Heading & Forging ↗

Heated stock can be formed into larger or heavier geometries before finishing operations define the final interfaces.

ROUTE 04 / HYBRID

Cold Heading + Secondary Machining ↗

A formed blank provides the basic shape; selected machined features establish critical steps, faces or holes.

01Material & blank02Forming route03Thread & features04Heat treatment*05Surface & cleaning06Verification

*Where required. Sequence varies with material, geometry and acceptance criteria; it is not a universal traveler.

02 / COMPLETE THE PART

The operations beyond the blank.

PROCESS / THREAD GENERATION

Thread Rolling, Cutting & Tapping ↗

The thread profile, material and batch conditions determine whether rolling, cutting, grinding or an internal tapping process is appropriate.

PROCESS / FUNCTIONAL FEATURES

Secondary & Precision Operations ↗

Local holes, flats, grooves and finished diameters often create the functional difference in a non-standard fastener.

PROCESS / MATERIAL CONDITION

Material-Specific Heat Treatment ↗

Heat-treatment selection follows the alloy, required condition and applicable acceptance specification. One sequence cannot be applied to every screw.

PROCESS / SURFACE SYSTEM

Coatings & Surface Treatments ↗

Specify a complete surface system: substrate condition, coating, thickness, functional surfaces and acceptance criteria.

PROCESS / FINAL CONDITION

Cleaning, Locking & Assembly ↗

Cleanliness, burr control and pre-applied features are part of the finished-part specification, not an afterthought.

PROCESS / ACCEPTANCE

CCD Vision & Dimensional Inspection ↗

Non-contact optical checks for screw length, head diameter and visible stepped profiles, combined with the gauges and tests required by the drawing.

Quote the complete chain.

Include material grade, final condition, drive, thread, critical fits, finish, cleaning, locking features, sample approval and inspection records.

Prepare your RFQ ↗

Confirm the route for the drawing.

Process coverage is reviewed for the actual part. Equipment ownership, partner operations, size limits and test arrangements are confirmed during quotation rather than inferred from a process name.

DRAWING TO ACCEPTANCE

Define the check.
Agree the evidence.

Build the inspection plan around functional features, risk and the acceptance requirements of the actual order.

What an inspection record should let you verify ↓

Dimensions & geometry

Shoulders, lengths, datum relationships, position, eccentricity, runout and surface texture.

Review the relevant process ↗

Thread acceptance

The specified thread designation, fit, usable engagement and appropriate GO/NO-GO checks.

Review the relevant process ↗

Material & condition

Material evidence, specified HV/HRC hardness, strength and heat-treatment documentation.

Review the relevant process ↗

Surface & cleanliness

Coating thickness, agreed corrosion tests, burrs and specified cleanliness extraction/particle criteria.

Review the relevant process ↗

Functional & specialist tests

Torque, tensile, fatigue, metallography or hydrogen evaluation where the application calls for them.

Review the relevant process ↗

Records & approval

Drawing revision, agreed sampling, first-article/sample approval, traceability and requested reports.

Review the relevant process ↗

Full inspection where it is justified.

Agree which features need 100% screening and which use an approved sampling plan. Full dimensional screening does not replace material or destructive test requirements.

CCD optical dimensional inspection, thread gauges and mechanical testing address different characteristics. Non-contact silhouette measurement supports accessible external features; internal geometry and other requirements need appropriate complementary methods. Availability and any external laboratory arrangements are confirmed in the quotation.

Prepare the inspection plan ↗

Precision means a defined requirement.

Specify the fit and surface condition rather than assuming one machining method is mandatory. Distinguish shaft fits such as g6/h7 from thread classes such as 6g/6H.

Explore verification methods ↗

Product photographs supplied for this website

These reference photographs show visible product forms. They do not establish material grade, dimensions, inspection results or a delivered customer application.

Set three clear release checkpoints

Use the drawing revision and characteristic IDs to keep sample approval, lot acceptance and change approval connected. Agree the records required for the order before production.

Approve the sample basis

Identify the drawing revision, sample route, critical characteristics and mating-part reference. Record whether the submission contains measured values, screening results, material documents or an assembly trial.

Accept the lot in its supplied condition

For each characteristic, agree the method, stage, coverage and record. Keep individual measurements distinct from pass/fail screening, and specify any external test report separately.

Resolve changes and deviations

Record the affected requirement, proposed disposition and approval before release. If the drawing, route or finish changes, identify which checks and sample approvals must be repeated.

Build a characteristic-by-characteristic inspection plan ↗

What an inspection record should let you verify

Build a traceable chain from each drawing requirement to the method, result and disposition. The downloadable forms below are planning templates; they contain no claimed production measurements.

What an inspection record should let you verify
ApplicationWhat to specifyWhat to check
Dimensional recordPart and drawing revision, lot, characteristic, limits, method/instrument identity, coverage and actual result.Distinguish recorded measurements from an agreed pass/fail screening result.
Material or treatment recordMaterial or treatment specification, lot reference and the documents or tests agreed for that requirement.Keep material identity, final hardness/strength and coating evidence distinguishable.
Assembly trialMating-part revision, installation method, functional criterion, outcome and approver.Record deviations and disposition; a dimensional pass does not establish assembly performance.

For example, CCD screening can evaluate a visible shoulder profile, a thread gauge addresses its specified thread requirement, and a material record addresses a different question again. Agree the relevant methods and any external test arrangements for the order; the template does not assert that every test is performed in-house.

What to include in a custom screw RFQ

A useful quotation starts with a clear specification. A drawing is the best starting point, but a sample, sketch or assembly description can also help define the next questions.

By Theo Wan • ZUFEK Technical Editorial • Published October 29, 2026
IN THIS GUIDEStart with the drawing and revisionIdentify the features that matterSpecify material and finish separatelyInclude quantity and delivery contextYour RFQ checklistSeparate mandatory requirements from discussion itemsUse a quotation comparison sheetClose the review with a release decision
RELATED PRODUCTCustom Metal Screws ↗

Start with the drawing and revision

Include the drawing number, revision, units and quantity. Show overall length, thread specification, head dimensions and any shoulders. If a requirement is still open, label it as open rather than leaving it ambiguous.

Identify the features that matter

Mark dimensions that affect fit or function. Explain the mating part, assembly access and service conditions. A tolerance on every surface may create unnecessary cost; let functional needs guide the discussion.

Working on this type of part? Explore our custom metal screws and include the functional requirements in your RFQ.

Specify material and finish separately

State a material grade if it is known. Identify any coating, appearance or corrosion requirements separately. A material family or a finish name alone may not be enough to define an acceptance requirement.

Include quantity and delivery context

Provide prototype quantity, initial order quantity and expected repeat demand if available. Include the destination and requested date. Lead time and feasibility need confirmation after technical review.

Your RFQ checklist

Drawing or sketch • revision and units • material • finish • critical features • quantity • inspection documents • destination. Downloading a checklist is optional: you can paste these details directly into the quotation form.

Separate mandatory requirements from discussion items

Mark the interfaces that must remain unchanged: mating thread, locating diameter, bearing face and available installation envelope. Identify other features as open for review where that is true. A supplier can then propose a manufacturing change without silently changing the assembly function. If a drawing note conflicts with a model or sample, record the controlling requirement before obtaining a production quotation.

Use a quotation comparison sheet

Compare the same drawing revision and quantities. List one-time tooling, samples, recurring parts, treatment, inspection records, packaging and delivery terms separately. Ask each proposal to identify exclusions and deviations. A price for a blank that excludes a critical finishing operation is not equivalent to a price for an accepted finished part.

Close the review with a release decision

The quotation review should end with an agreed specification, confirmed sample quantity, schedule basis and acceptance plan. Typical tooling and sampling is approximately 10–15 days, subject to review. Repeat-production delivery is separate. Keep unresolved points visible so an early commercial estimate is not mistaken for an approved manufacturing release.

Ready to discuss your part?

Use the RFQ preparation checklist, then submit your drawing for review. For acceptance requirements, see quality planning.

A practical guide to shoulder screw drawings

A shoulder screw drawing needs separate bore-fit, axial-stack, thread and final-surface requirements. Check both tolerance limits before sample approval.

By Theo Wan • ZUFEK Technical Editorial • Published October 29, 2026 · Updated 2026-11-03
IN THIS GUIDEDefine the shoulderShow how the thread endsReview head access and seatingCommunicate functional tolerancesDraw the assembly stack, not only the screwChoose datums that match the locating functionApprove the final supplied surfaceWorked review: calculate diametral clearance separately
RELATED PRODUCTShoulder & Step Screws ↗

Turn the diameter limits into a review record

Worked review only. Inputs and acceptance criteria belong to the actual drawing; no customer test result or universal performance rating is claimed.

Minimum diametral clearance
8.010 − 8.005 = 0.005 mm, using the smallest bore and largest shoulder.
Maximum diametral clearance
8.030 − 7.995 = 0.035 mm, using the largest bore and smallest shoulder.
Shoulder interfaces and the separate axial-clearance example ↗

Define the shoulder

Dimension shoulder diameter and shoulder length independently from thread length. Explain whether the shoulder serves as a locating surface, bearing surface or spacer. The functional role helps identify which features need closer review.

Show how the thread ends

State thread designation and length, and show any relief or transition at the shoulder. Check how the screw seats in the mating assembly. Do not assume the end of the usable thread is identical to the end of the visible thread form.

Working on this type of part? Explore our shoulder & step screws and include the functional requirements in your RFQ.

Review head access and seating

Include head diameter, height and drive configuration. Consider the tool clearance and seating surface in the assembly. A head that fits the drawing may still be inaccessible once neighboring parts are installed.

Communicate functional tolerances

Mark the mating bore relationship and any surface finish requirement that affects motion or fit. Tolerances should be established by the application engineer and confirmed during manufacturing review.

Draw the assembly stack, not only the screw

Show the seating face, moving component, washer or bushing and intended axial clearance. Dimension the shoulder length against this stack. If the shoulder is too short, tightening can clamp the moving part; too long can leave excessive movement. Review the worst permitted stack before approving shoulder length, rather than adjusting it after a binding prototype is received.

Choose datums that match the locating function

Identify the axis and face that locate the part in service. Decide whether shoulder form, runout or another specified relationship affects the mechanism. Listing only outside diameters can leave the functional relationship undefined. Agree how the relationship is checked, particularly if the part is located differently during successive machining operations.

Approve the final supplied surface

Treatment and coating may change the condition used to accept the shoulder. State final limits and coating coverage on the functional surface. The inspection record should distinguish shoulder measurement from thread gauging. A correct thread does not establish that the pivot fits, and a correct external silhouette does not establish surface texture.

Worked review: calculate diametral clearance separately

Assume a finished shoulder diameter of 8.000 ± 0.005 mm and a mating bore of 8.020 ± 0.010 mm. Compare the smallest bore with the largest shoulder, then the largest bore with the smallest shoulder. The resulting 0.005–0.035 mm range is diametral clearance, not radial clearance or an axial gap. These illustrative inputs do not define a standard fit or an approved operating range. The designer still specifies the functional range, temperature basis, datum relationships and final surface condition.

Five questions before specifying a captive screw

Specify a captive screw with its panel, retainer and mating thread. Review installation, released travel and tightened engagement as separate conditions.

By Theo Wan • ZUFEK Technical Editorial • Published October 29, 2026 · Updated 2026-11-03
IN THIS GUIDEWhat retains the screw?How much movement is needed?What happens during service?How will the assembly be verified?What should accompany the RFQ?Worked review: release a service panel without losing the screw
RELATED PRODUCTCaptive Screws ↗

Keep the two service positions in the approval record

Worked review only. Inputs and acceptance criteria belong to the actual drawing; no customer test result or universal performance rating is claimed.

Assembly sketch to supply
Panel thickness and hole, retaining part, open and tightened positions, thread engagement and nearby obstructions.
Sample review to agree
Identify the panel, retainer and screw revisions; record retention, release clearance and reassembly against their separate criteria.
Open and tightened captive-screw interface sketch ↗

What retains the screw?

Describe the intended retaining component or geometry. Provide an assembly view and panel details. The screw alone does not establish whether the completed assembly will remain captive.

How much movement is needed?

Show required travel, open position and thread engagement. Explain how the operator installs and releases the fastener, including available access.

Working on this type of part? Explore our captive screws and include the functional requirements in your RFQ.

What happens during service?

Describe repeated access, vibration, cleaning and exposure conditions. These inputs inform the material, finish and design discussion; they do not replace assembly testing.

How will the assembly be verified?

Define retention and functional acceptance criteria with your engineering team. A dimensional inspection and an assembly test answer different questions.

What should accompany the RFQ?

Include the screw drawing, mating assembly, quantity and any sample photos. Unresolved retention details can be reviewed before a final quotation is issued.

Worked review: release a service panel without losing the screw

For a service-panel design exercise, begin with the intended installation sequence. Show how the screw and retaining part are assembled, which feature prevents escape after release, and where the screw sits once tightened. Check that the available released travel clears the mating thread and permits the panel to open. Then check that the retained hardware does not obstruct seating or reduce the required engagement. Record retention and opening/reassembly as separate checks against the identified panel and retainer revisions.

Choosing material for a custom metal screw

Material selection begins with the service environment and mechanical requirements. The best specification balances function, manufacturability, availability and verification.

By Theo Wan • ZUFEK Technical Editorial • Published October 29, 2026
IN THIS GUIDEDescribe the environment firstDefine the mechanical requirementsTreat finish as part of the systemConfirm documentation needsCompare alternatives against one requirement setCheck the cost of the finished conditionApprove substitutions deliberately
RELATED PRODUCTCustom Metal Screws ↗

Describe the environment first

State whether the part will encounter moisture, chemicals, heat or outdoor exposure. Include contact with dissimilar metals and any cleaning process. Avoid choosing a grade based on appearance alone.

Define the mechanical requirements

Provide the applicable strength, hardness or other performance requirements where relevant. Different grades and processing conditions can behave differently; a material family alone is not a complete mechanical specification.

Working on this type of part? Explore our custom metal screws and include the functional requirements in your RFQ.

Treat finish as part of the system

Coatings may influence dimensions, friction and assembly behavior. Identify the required finish and the surfaces on which it matters. Allowances should be reviewed against the drawing and actual process.

Confirm documentation needs

Tell the supplier whether you require material documentation, inspection records or other supporting evidence. Confirm availability and acceptance requirements before placing an order.

Compare alternatives against one requirement set

Prepare a comparison covering finished mechanical requirements, environment, mating metals, thread engagement, mass, surface and required evidence. Compare grade and condition together. A stock tensile figure for one alloy and a finished fastener class for another do not provide a like-for-like comparison.

Check the cost of the finished condition

Include treatment, secondary machining, finishing allowance and inspection in the comparison. An alloy that appears inexpensive as stock may require a different manufacturing route or surface process. Ask the quotation to identify the proposed final condition so a price comparison does not hide a different technical scope.

Approve substitutions deliberately

A replacement grade or temper can change forming, strength, contact or finishing behavior. Confirm the actual supplied specification and required documentation before approving it. Keep the decision with the drawing revision and repeat-order record. Similar appearance alone does not establish that a substitute meets the same function.

Geometry and manufacturing route

Head shape, length ratios, steps, internal features and thread configuration affect the manufacturing options. Feasibility needs review against the actual drawing and available processes.

Tolerance and inspection

Tighter requirements can change processing and measurement effort. Identify truly critical dimensions so the review focuses on the features that drive function.

Working on this type of part? Explore our special head screws and include the functional requirements in your RFQ.

Material, finish and order volume

Material grade, secondary operations, finish requirements and batch size affect the quotation. Prototype and repeat production quantities may have different cost structures.

Discuss changes before revising

Separate recurring operations from one-time investment

Identify tooling, setup, sample production, unit processing, inspection and packaging. Ask how recurring cost changes at the intended batch sizes while keeping the drawing constant. Compare the total accepted finished-part scope; a lower price that excludes a required local feature or verification is not an equivalent offer.

Identify the cost-driving feature before changing it

Ask which tolerance, geometry or finish creates additional operations. A controlled shoulder, internal passage or unusual recess can affect different stages. The designer should decide whether a proposed change preserves the interface and function. Do not relax several dimensions simply to reduce a quotation when only one feature drives the cost.

Quote the transition from sample to repeat supply

State whether tooling is required, how samples are approved and what is included in a repeat order. Typical sampling including tooling is approximately 10–15 days, subject to review and confirmation. Confirm production delivery separately and record the approved drawing, route and quality scope so future comparisons use the same basis.

How to prepare an inspection plan for custom screws

Build an inspection plan one characteristic at a time. For each drawing requirement, record the acceptance condition, a suitable method, the inspection stage and coverage, and the evidence retained. The worked rows below show how to turn a shoulder-screw drawing into an inspection record.

By Theo Wan • ZUFEK Technical Editorial • Published October 29, 2026 · Updated 2026-11-02
IN THIS GUIDEStart with the released requirementUse the example without copying a test scope blindlyDefine coverage and reaction before productionRecord the result and the release decision
RELATED PRODUCTShoulder & Step Screws ↗

Worked inspection-plan matrix

Illustrative planning rows, not measured results. Insert the actual drawing requirements and agreed inspection coverage before release.

Shoulder-screw inspection-plan example
CharacteristicRequirement to enterSuitable evidenceCoverage and record
C1 · Shoulder diameterApproved drawing limits; final supplied conditionCalibrated diameter measurement; validated vision only if suitableAgreed sample or every-piece scope; record actual values or the approved screening result
C2 · Shoulder lengthDistance from the functional seating faceLength measurement from the specified face, with a documented setupLink the result to the drawing revision and lot
C3 · Thread acceptanceThread system, pitch, class and usable lengthAppropriate gauges plus a separate usable-length check when requiredRecord gauge identity and the agreed acceptance result
C4 · Geometric runout, if specifiedDatum, controlled surface and tolerance on the drawingA datum-referenced setup that measures the specified relationshipA diameter-only camera result does not replace this check
C5 · Material and finishOrdered grade, condition and treatment requirementsAgreed documents and applicable physical or coating checksKeep stock certificates, final-part results and coating records distinguishable
C6 · Assembly functionApproved mating-part revision and functional criteriaControlled assembly trial for movement, seating or retentionRecord the mating reference, outcome, deviations and approver

Download the example inspection plan (English) · Download a blank inspection worksheet (English)

Start with the released requirement

Record the part number, drawing revision, order or lot, material condition and supplied finish. Resolve conflicting dimensions and undefined notes before selecting equipment. The example matrix deliberately uses drawing references instead of invented production limits. Replace those references with the approved requirements for the actual part.

Use the example without copying a test scope blindly

A shoulder diameter, a thread and a material property require different evidence. A camera may screen a visible profile after validation, but it does not establish material strength or every datum relationship. A thread gauge does not establish shoulder length. Keep these characteristics in separate rows even when one production station performs several checks.

Working on this type of part? Explore our shoulder & step screws and include the functional requirements in your RFQ.

Define coverage and reaction before production

For each row, agree first-article, sampled or every-piece coverage and the point in the route where acceptance is measured. A destructive check cannot be applied to every delivered piece in the same way as a dimensional screen. Define how a failed or borderline result is identified, segregated and reviewed, including which work or shipment must stop pending disposition.

Record the result and the release decision

Use the blank worksheet to capture requirement, actual value or agreed pass/fail result, instrument or method reference, inspector, date and disposition. A sample report should identify the mating part used for any assembly trial. When the drawing or finish changes, review the affected rows and preserve the previous revision rather than silently editing an old result.

Specification example

Worked example only: an external shoulder size is checked after finishing, while thread acceptance uses the specified gauges and an assembly trial checks that the moving plate is not clamped. The example establishes record fields, not numerical limits, completed measurements or a ZUFEK inspection result.

RFQ checklist

  • Part, drawing revision and lot identity
  • Characteristic and approved acceptance requirement
  • Method, stage and coverage
  • Actual result and traceable record
  • Nonconformance disposition and release approval

Cold heading or CNC turning: choosing a custom screw route

Choose the manufacturing route around geometry, quantity, material and required condition. A lower cycle cost does not always offset tooling or secondary work.

By Theo Wan • ZUFEK Technical Editorial • Published October 29, 2026
IN THIS GUIDEStart with the repeat volumeSeparate bulk shape from functional detailCheck the material and acceptance requirementsReview the complete routeBuild a route comparison around the same finished specificationAsk what changes between prototype and productionResolve geometry before committing tooling
RELATED PRODUCTCustom Metal Screws ↗

Start with the repeat volume

Cold heading can be economical for repeated geometries at a suitable volume, while CNC turning can offer flexible setup for prototypes and varying features. The actual break-even point needs a quotation for the drawing, not a universal quantity rule.

Separate bulk shape from functional detail

A head and rough shoulder may suit forming, while a bore, flat or critical shoulder needs machining. A hybrid route should be costed as a complete sequence rather than comparing only the first operation.

Working on this type of part? Explore our custom metal screws and include the functional requirements in your RFQ.

Check the material and acceptance requirements

Formability, stock condition and required final properties influence both routes. Machining is not universally weaker than cold heading: material, geometry, heat treatment and load case determine performance.

Review the complete route

Include thread generation, any treatment, precision finishing, coating, cleaning and inspection. Specify which dimensions are functional so the proposed process protects the relevant datums and fits.

Build a route comparison around the same finished specification

List stock preparation, primary shape, local features, threading, treatment, finishing and verification for each option. Record which operations remain after forming. Compare tooling and recurring costs separately at realistic order quantities. There is no universal order quantity at which a complex cold-headed part becomes cheaper than its machined alternative.

Ask what changes between prototype and production

A machined sample can help review assembly, but does not automatically validate a later formed route. Identify whether material condition, local radii, surface condition or final properties differ. Agree which checks must be repeated on parts from the intended production route before relying on a prototype approval.

Resolve geometry before committing tooling

A change to head shape, a drive recess or a step can affect tooling differently from a change to a turned feature. Review likely drawing changes before authorizing tooling. Where uncertainty remains, agree what the samples are intended to demonstrate and which production decisions remain open. This separates an assembly concept trial from approval of a complete manufacturing route.

MATERIALS & FINISHES / 2 MIN READ

High-strength screw coatings and hydrogen-risk review

A high-strength steel fastener needs a coating decision that considers both corrosion and hydrogen exposure throughout processing.

By Theo Wan • ZUFEK Technical Editorial • Published October 29, 2026
IN THIS GUIDEIdentify the susceptible conditionDefine a coating systemUnderstand the limit of bakingWrite a useful RFQMap potential exposure through the full routeDefine evidence before the orderKeep corrosion, friction and fit in the same review
RELATED PRODUCTShoulder & Step Screws ↗

Identify the susceptible condition

Strength, hardness, material condition and tensile stress influence susceptibility. Cleaning, pickling and electroplating can be hydrogen sources. Property class alone is not a complete risk assessment.

Define a coating system

Specify the substrate, process, coating thickness, friction and acceptance requirements. Zinc-flake deposition can avoid electrolytic deposition, but pretreatment and other steps must still be reviewed.

Working on this type of part? Explore our shoulder & step screws and include the functional requirements in your RFQ.

Understand the limit of baking

Hydrogen-relief baking can reduce risk under a controlled specification. It is not a guarantee that every fastener is free from embrittlement. Define any required process controls and verification with the responsible technical team.

Write a useful RFQ

Include grade, final properties, coating specification, functional fits, documentation and application requirements. Avoid a blanket rule that every zinc finish is forbidden or that every coating requires the same baking cycle.

Map potential exposure through the full route

Review cleaning and pretreatment alongside deposition. A non-electrolytic coating does not remove every possible hydrogen source elsewhere in the sequence. Relate the process to the specified material condition and application stress. Avoid treating either a coating trade name or a property-class label as a complete risk assessment.

Define evidence before the order

The responsible technical review should establish the applicable process controls, any relief requirement, verification and records. A generic statement that parts were baked omits the conditions that made the process applicable. Risk reduction is not a guarantee of elimination; decide the acceptance scope under the actual specification rather than substituting a blanket zinc ban or blanket bake instruction.

Keep corrosion, friction and fit in the same review

Changing a coating to address one concern can alter thread allowance, friction or the bearing surface. Reassess the assembly and dimensional requirements when the surface system changes. A corrosion test result under stated conditions does not prove field life or the absence of embrittlement. These are different acceptance questions.

MATERIALS & FINISHES / 2 MIN READ

304, 316 and 17-4PH: different heat-treatment questions

Stainless steel describes several material families. Specify the grade and final condition rather than writing one generic heat-treatment instruction.

By Theo Wan • ZUFEK Technical Editorial • Published October 29, 2026
IN THIS GUIDEDistinguish austenitic from precipitation-hardening gradesState the purpose of solution treatmentDefine the final condition of 17-4PHCoordinate finish and verificationResolve what the drawing means by high-strength stainlessSeparate material treatment from surface treatmentReview assembly galling as a separate mechanism
RELATED PRODUCTCustom Metal Screws ↗

Distinguish austenitic from precipitation-hardening grades

304 and 316 are austenitic stainless steels and are not hardened by the precipitation-aging treatment used for 17-4PH. They can strengthen through cold work, which must be considered separately from heat treatment.

State the purpose of solution treatment

Solution annealing and stress-related treatments have material-specific purposes and can affect corrosion behavior and dimensional condition. They should not be treated as a universal hardening cycle.

Working on this type of part? Explore our custom metal screws and include the functional requirements in your RFQ.

Define the final condition of 17-4PH

A precipitation-hardening grade requires an explicitly selected condition and corresponding property requirements. Do not assume that any aging cycle is interchangeable with another.

Coordinate finish and verification

Passivation is a surface treatment, not the same operation as solution treatment or precipitation hardening. State material evidence, final properties, critical dimensions and requested inspection records.

Resolve what the drawing means by high-strength stainless

Clarify whether the requirement names a finished fastener class or a specific alloy and condition. A change from an austenitic grade to 17-4PH changes the material specification as well as the treatment discussion. It needs approval against corrosion, mechanical and application requirements; it is not a manufacturing shortcut to apply without the designer.

Separate material treatment from surface treatment

Passivation addresses surface condition; it is not a replacement for the specified material condition. Keep material evidence, mechanical requirements and the surface process separately identifiable in the order. A visually similar surface does not prove that the correct alloy or final condition was supplied.

Review assembly galling as a separate mechanism

A selected stainless grade does not eliminate the need to review thread contact and the mating pair. Surface condition, assembly and lubrication can affect galling, and a lubrication change can also affect tightening behavior. Coordinate the assembly process with the approved specification instead of using an unqualified torque figure from another joint.

DESIGN & DIMENSIONS / 2 MIN READ

Shoulder fits, thread classes and when grinding matters

A shaft fit and a thread tolerance class control different interfaces. Write the required function clearly before deciding how the surfaces must be finished.

By Theo Wan • ZUFEK Technical Editorial • Published October 29, 2026
IN THIS GUIDESeparate the plain shoulder and the threadIdentify the mating relationshipSpecify grinding only with a reasonInspect after the relevant finishing stageCompare limits against the actual mating boreMake finishing selection a capability discussionRetain independent acceptance checks
RELATED PRODUCTShoulder & Step Screws ↗

Separate the plain shoulder and the thread

A shaft tolerance such as g6 or h7 describes a plain cylindrical feature. A designation such as 6g or 6H belongs to a metric thread tolerance system. Case and order matter; these are not interchangeable callouts.

Identify the mating relationship

Provide the mating bore, shoulder length, datums and surface texture. Clearance, locating behavior and rotation depend on both components and their operating conditions.

Working on this type of part? Explore our shoulder & step screws and include the functional requirements in your RFQ.

Specify grinding only with a reason

Grinding can be useful for size, form and surface finish, especially after a treatment that changes dimensions. A tolerance designation alone does not prove that centerless grinding is the only acceptable route.

Inspect after the relevant finishing stage

Review coating allowance and final condition. Agree measurement methods for size, form and datum relationships, together with thread gauging and the required inspection records.

Compare limits against the actual mating bore

Record the shoulder requirement beside the bore limits and operating purpose. Decide whether the joint needs clearance, location or motion and what acceptance condition applies. A shaft tolerance designation and a metric thread class refer to different features. Copying a thread class onto a plain shoulder does not describe the required fit.

Make finishing selection a capability discussion

Ask how the proposed route achieves size, form and surface requirements in the final condition. If heat treatment or coating follows an earlier size operation, consider its effect before approving the route. Grinding may be appropriate; the mere presence of a grinding operation does not prove that the specified relationship or finish has been achieved.

Retain independent acceptance checks

Check the shoulder using a suitable dimensional method and the thread using the applicable thread acceptance method. Where runout or another datum relationship is specified, verify that relationship directly. Do not substitute a diameter-only screen for a geometry requirement that the screen has not been shown to measure.

DESIGN & DIMENSIONS / 3 MIN READ

How to specify a tamper-resistant screw drive

Specify the drive profile, matching tool, finish and installed access together. A bit that fits a loose screw may still fail to engage inside the housing.

By Theo Wan • ZUFEK Technical Editorial • Published October 29, 2026 · Updated 2026-11-03
IN THIS GUIDEIdentify the exact interfaceDefine the head and tool accessReview pin and recess featuresSeparate access resistance from joint performanceWorked review: distinguish a tool-fit issue from an access issue
RELATED PRODUCTSecurity & Tamper-Resistant Screws ↗

Identify the interface that needs correction

Worked review only. Inputs and acceptance criteria belong to the actual drawing; no customer test result or universal performance rating is claimed.

Tool and loose-part record
Drive reference, bit identity, pin clearance and usable engagement on the finished sample.
Installed-access record
Housing revision, tool holder and approach envelope, access restriction and the proposed drawing change.
Security-drive and installed-tool access sketch ↗

Identify the exact interface

Pin-in six-lobe, five-lobe, Y-type, triangle and two-hole spanner designs are different interfaces. Even visually similar recesses can have incompatible profiles. Supply a controlled drive drawing, recognized interface reference or approved matching tool rather than asking a manufacturer to copy a small photograph.

Define the head and tool access

Head diameter, height and surrounding enclosure affect whether the intended tool can reach the recess. Show the assembled condition, including any counterbore or nearby wall. A usable loose screw can become difficult to service after it is installed inside the product.

Working on this type of part? Explore our security & tamper-resistant screws and include the functional requirements in your RFQ.

Review pin and recess features

For a center-pin drive, include the pin geometry, recess depth and relevant edge condition. Forming and secondary machining offer different ways to create these details. Inspect the functional tool engagement as well as the external head dimensions; a recess can look correct while fitting poorly.

Separate access resistance from joint performance

A special drive can discourage casual removal, but it does not make a joint impossible to open. Material, thread engagement and the tightening method still determine the mechanical connection. Define service access, installation torque requirements and the intended tool-control arrangement independently.

Worked review: distinguish a tool-fit issue from an access issue

Consider a pin-in screw in a recessed cover. First compare the finished recess with the identified service bit outside the housing. Next review the same bit in the installed position, including its holder and approach space. If engagement is satisfactory outside but restricted inside, review the access envelope before changing the drive profile. If the bit cannot seat in either position, review the recess, pin, bit and final finish together. Record which interface changed and repeat the affected check with the same controlled tool reference.

Specification example

For an enclosure fastener, supply the enclosure recess and service-tool outline alongside the screw drawing. This allows the quotation review to consider drive engagement and access together before tooling is selected.

  • Drive drawing or approved tool
  • Head envelope and access clearance
  • Pin and recess dimensions
  • Material, finish and quantity
  • Functional tool-fit acceptance

Hollow screw bores: the details an RFQ should include

Specify the complete bore, minimum remaining wall, internal edges and acceptance method. Use thread-root geometry and bore offset in the section review.

By Theo Wan • ZUFEK Technical Editorial • Published October 29, 2026 · Updated 2026-11-03
IN THIS GUIDEDescribe the entire passageReview wall thickness with the threadState edge and cleanliness requirementsDefine functional tests separatelyWorked review: include bore offset in the wall calculation
RELATED PRODUCTHollow & Through-Hole Screws ↗

Record the limiting section and the inspection access

Worked review only. Inputs and acceptance criteria belong to the actual drawing; no customer test result or universal performance rating is claimed.

Section result
1.30 mm is the calculated remaining wall for the stated teaching inputs, not a safe-wall recommendation or pressure rating.
Separate internal-edge decision
Identify the intersecting hole and burr requirement, the deburring stage and a suitable check before later assembly limits access.
Hollow-screw section and passage review ↗

Describe the entire passage

Identify whether the hole is through, blind, stepped or connected to a side passage. Dimension each section and its axial position. A single opening diameter does not define an internal path, and a photograph cannot establish hidden counterbores or restrictions.

Review wall thickness with the thread

The bore and external thread share the same material section. Show their relationship through the thinnest region and identify any concentricity or position requirement. Manufacturing review needs the actual geometry; an outside diameter alone is not sufficient to evaluate a hollow threaded feature.

Working on this type of part? Explore our hollow & through-hole screws and include the functional requirements in your RFQ.

State edge and cleanliness requirements

Drilling can leave burrs at hole exits and intersections. Specify which edges must be broken and how internal burrs will be accepted. If the part carries fluid, adhesive or a wire, explain the relevant contamination, surface-damage or blockage concern rather than relying on a generic clean note.

Define functional tests separately

A continuous bore does not itself prove pressure capability, leak tightness or unrestricted flow in an assembly. State any test medium, fixture arrangement and acceptance method that the application requires. These conditions should be agreed before sampling so manufacturing and inspection can be quoted together.

Worked review: include bore offset in the wall calculation

For an illustrative circular section, take a lower-limit thread-root envelope diameter of 6.00 mm, an upper-limit bore diameter of 3.00 mm and a maximum radial bore-centre offset of 0.20 mm. The minimum remaining wall in that section is (6.00 − 3.00) ÷ 2 − 0.20 = 1.30 mm. The offset is a radial distance here, not a diametral position-tolerance callout. This calculation does not cover cross-hole intersections, other local sections or load capacity. Derive the actual inputs from the controlled geometry and its tolerance limits.

Specification example

For a screw used as a cable passage, show the cable envelope and the edges it contacts. For a fluid passage, describe the intended sealing interface separately from the through hole.

RFQ checklist

  • Complete bore section
  • Minimum wall and feature relationship
  • Hole exit and intersection burr limits
  • Internal cleanliness requirements
  • Required functional test method

Designing the bearing face of a custom flange screw

Match the flange bearing face to the actual supporting surface. Compare the contact footprint, finish and grip length before replacing a separate washer.

By Theo Wan • ZUFEK Technical Editorial • Published October 29, 2026 · Updated 2026-11-03
IN THIS GUIDEStart with the mating surfaceDimension the flange as a functional featureChoose the face condition deliberatelyInclude the finish and tightening conditionsWorked review: compare an integral flange with a washer assembly
RELATED PRODUCTCustom Flange Screws ↗

Separate unchanged inputs from the proposed change

Worked review only. Inputs and acceptance criteria belong to the actual drawing; no customer test result or universal performance rating is claimed.

Keep the comparison basis
Bracket and slot revision, mating material, coating, assembly method and agreed acceptance criteria.
Compare the two arrangements
Supported footprint, transition clearance, washer contribution to grip length, engagement and marking after the agreed service sequence.
Smooth flange, serrated flange and separate-washer sketch ↗

Start with the mating surface

Identify the material beneath the flange and the available contact area. A soft panel, coated bracket and rigid machined seat respond differently. Show holes, slots and nearby edges so the bearing footprint can be reviewed against the real supporting surface.

Dimension the flange as a functional feature

Specify diameter, thickness and the transition beneath the head. Include flatness or surface requirements when they affect contact. Thin flanges and large overhangs should not be assumed to distribute load uniformly; their behavior needs review with the intended connection and material condition.

Working on this type of part? Explore our custom flange screws and include the functional requirements in your RFQ.

Choose the face condition deliberately

Plain, textured and serrated bearing faces are not interchangeable. A serration may change the contact behavior and affect a coating or soft surface. Explain whether the priority is appearance, resistance to movement, contact pressure or another function, then agree the relevant acceptance checks.

Include the finish and tightening conditions

Coating thickness and friction can influence the assembled joint. Treat the flange face and threads as specified surfaces, not simply parts of an overall color requirement. Any comparison with a washer assembly should consider the complete joint rather than the number of handled components.

Worked review: compare an integral flange with a washer assembly

For a coated slotted bracket, compare the existing head-and-washer arrangement with the proposed integral flange on the same bracket drawing. Identify the supporting surface left around the slot and the areas that must remain clear. Review flange or washer overhang, the under-head transition and permissible coating marks. Account for the washer thickness when comparing grip length and usable engagement. Keep the assembly method and acceptance criteria explicit; fewer loose components do not establish equivalent bearing behavior or retained clamp load.

Specification example

When replacing a loose washer with an integral flange, provide both assembly drawings. The review should compare the supporting footprint and seating condition before treating the two arrangements as equivalent.

RFQ checklist

  • Mating material and hole shape
  • Flange diameter and thickness
  • Bearing-face condition
  • Clearance and finish requirements
  • Assembly acceptance criteria

Knurled thumb screws: specifying grip and adjustment

A hand-adjusted screw must be accessible, comfortable to grip and compatible with the required adjustment. Head texture alone does not define how the mechanism works.

By Theo Wan • ZUFEK Technical Editorial • Published October 29, 2026
IN THIS GUIDEDescribe the way it is operatedSpecify the knurl rather than an appearanceConnect pitch to the adjustment requirementDecide whether a service drive is needed
RELATED PRODUCTKnurled Thumb & Adjustment Screws ↗

Describe the way it is operated

Explain whether the user adjusts the part frequently, wears gloves or works in a restricted space. Head diameter and height influence access as much as the knurl pattern. Include surrounding components so the manufacturer can review usable grip clearance rather than only the isolated head.

Specify the knurl rather than an appearance

Straight and diamond patterns provide different textures. State the required head envelope and any controlled pattern details. Agree acceptable surface and edge condition, especially where users handle the component repeatedly. A reference sample can support the discussion, but the approved requirements should be recorded.

Working on this type of part? Explore our knurled thumb & adjustment screws and include the functional requirements in your RFQ.

Connect pitch to the adjustment requirement

Describe the required travel, mating thread and any backlash or position-holding concern. Fine pitch may provide smaller movement per turn, but the complete mechanism determines useful adjustment. Specify a separate locking feature if the setting must remain stable under service conditions.

Decide whether a service drive is needed

A slot or socket may supplement hand operation, but it can introduce a different tightening method. Clarify how each interface is intended to be used. Do not assume a hand-grip feature establishes a controlled tightening torque or prevents the operator from overloading the assembly.

Specification example

For an adjustable fixture stop, include the usable adjustment range and the contact surface at the tip. This helps separate grip design from the positioning and locking functions.

RFQ checklist

  • Available finger and tool clearance
  • Head dimensions and knurl pattern
  • Adjustment travel and mating thread
  • Locking or retention arrangement
  • Surface and edge acceptance

Cone, flat, dog or cup: choosing a set-screw tip

Choose a set-screw point by its contact with the mating part. Define allowable marking, adjustment and retention, then verify the complete joint.

By Theo Wan • ZUFEK Technical Editorial • Published October 29, 2026 · Updated 2026-11-03
IN THIS GUIDEChoose the contact mechanism firstWork through an adjustable-stop exampleSeparate location from frictional clampingRelease a point and a verification planWrite a repeat-adjustment acceptance record
RELATED PRODUCTCustom Set Screws & Grub Screws ↗

Compare the four contact mechanisms

Set-screw point selection: geometry and trade-offs
Point formContactWhen to review itWhat to verify
Flat pointA broad end face bears against a prepared flat or pad.Review for adjustments where a sharp biting edge is undesirable.It can still mark the mating surface. Check flat alignment, contact pressure and retention.
Cone pointA pointed end engages a suitable recess or indents the mating surface.Review for a defined setting where penetration or a mating recess is acceptable.Repeated relocation can damage the contact area. Define the cone and the mating feature.
Dog pointA cylindrical extension enters a prepared hole or slot.Review when the extension must locate or guide a component.Specify projection, diameter, clearance and available depth; do not let the point bottom unintentionally.
Cup pointThe rim of a recessed end makes concentrated contact.Review for a setting where an indentation is acceptable.Do not assume an undamaged surface after removal, or infer a universal holding force from the point name.

Compare the contact mechanism first; confirm capacity and installation on the actual joint.

Download the point-selection worksheet (English)

Make the adjustment trial repeatable

Worked review only. Inputs and acceptance criteria belong to the actual drawing; no customer test result or universal performance rating is claimed.

Before the trial
Point and pad drawings, permitted marking, adjustment travel and the agreed retained-setting criterion.
After the service sequence
Starting and returned positions, contact condition and outcome against each criterion; identify the point, pad and drawing revisions.
Set-screw contact forms in the mating assembly ↗

Choose the contact mechanism first

A point name describes geometry, not the holding capacity of the completed joint. Use the comparison below to shortlist a contact mechanism. Then provide the mating material and hardness, the prepared flat, recess or hole, and the intended adjustment and release procedure. A flat point is worth reviewing when a sharp biting edge is undesirable; it does not guarantee a mark-free shaft. A cone or cup can indent the mating surface. A dog point needs a defined mating hole or slot.

Work through an adjustable-stop example

Consider a fixture stop that is reset between jobs and contacts a finished pad. This is a design exercise, not a delivered customer case. First decide whether indentation is acceptable. If it is not, review broad-face contact and the pad material before selecting a point. Check alignment throughout the adjustment travel: a nominally flat end can contact on an edge if the screw approaches at an angle.

Working on this type of part? Explore our custom set screws & grub screws and include the functional requirements in your RFQ.

Separate location from frictional clamping

If a cylindrical dog enters a hole, show its projection and the available hole depth. Decide whether that extension locates the part, guides its movement or transmits a defined load. Provide clearance for the intended motion and check the installation sequence. Do not assume that an extension in a hole is an approved shear connection or that tightening the screw establishes the required retention by itself.

Release a point and a verification plan

Show the thread, drive access, overall length, point dimensions, final material condition and surface treatment on the controlled drawing. Agree installation requirements and a functional trial on a representative mating component. Record permitted marking and the behavior after the required adjustment or service sequence. No general torque or holding-force value is supplied here: those depend on the actual joint.

Write a repeat-adjustment acceptance record

For the fixture-stop exercise, define the starting setting, allowed contact mark and adjustment/service sequence before the trial. Check contact at both ends of travel and after returning to the starting setting. Record whether each result is a visual assessment, a dimensional reading or a functional observation. If the pad or point geometry changes, compare against the same criteria rather than reusing the old result. This creates an acceptance record; it does not establish a universal tightening torque or holding force.

Specification example

Illustrative review outcome: a repeat-adjusted stop uses a prepared contact pad and a defined end face. The trial checks contact throughout travel, visible marking and retention of the setting under the agreed conditions. Dimensions, material, torque and loads remain project inputs; no test result is claimed.

RFQ checklist

  • Point form and controlled geometry
  • Mating surface, recess or hole drawing
  • Allowed marking and adjustment sequence
  • Thread engagement, access and installation requirements
  • Dimensional and functional acceptance criteria

T-slot bolt fit: what to measure before ordering

A T-head must enter, turn or slide inside the intended slot while retaining the required contact. The slot cross-section is therefore an essential part of the fastener RFQ.

By Theo Wan • ZUFEK Technical Editorial • Published October 29, 2026
IN THIS GUIDEProvide the complete slot sectionExplain the insertion methodReview contact and anti-rotationCheck the finished condition
RELATED PRODUCTCustom T-Slot Bolts ↗

Provide the complete slot section

Measure the opening, internal width, depth and any corner radii. Explain which dimensions are controlled and whether the profile varies along the assembly. A nominal extrusion family or a top-view photograph may leave important internal clearances undefined.

Explain the insertion method

Some heads enter from a slot end; others must pass through the opening and rotate. These are different geometric requirements. Show the intended assembly sequence and any end stops or surrounding parts that prevent the movement assumed during installation.

Working on this type of part? Explore our custom t-slot bolts and include the functional requirements in your RFQ.

Review contact and anti-rotation

Head thickness, bearing faces and neck geometry influence how the bolt seats in the slot. Specify the required clearances and contact surfaces. A head that can be inserted is not automatically suitable for the required clamping load or resistance to rotation.

Check the finished condition

Coating and edge finishing can alter the available clearance. Agree the final head envelope and inspect the relevant features after finishing. A trial fit in an approved mating section may be useful, but it should support clearly documented dimensional and functional requirements.

Specification example

For a bolt that must rotate inside an aluminum profile, provide the rotation envelope as well as the installed position. This identifies interference that a single assembled view may hide.

RFQ checklist

  • Slot cross-section and radii
  • Insertion and rotation sequence
  • Head and neck clearances
  • Finished coating allowance
  • Agreed fit and clamping checks

Eye bolts for linkages and lifting: different specification needs

An eye-shaped end can belong to a linkage, a tensioning device or a lifting component. Similar appearance does not establish the same design requirements or approved use.

By Theo Wan • ZUFEK Technical Editorial • Published October 29, 2026
IN THIS GUIDEDefine the intended function firstShow the articulation and load directionTreat lifting requirements explicitlyPrepare a complete manufacturing review
RELATED PRODUCTCustom Eye & Articulating Bolts ↗

Define the intended function first

State how the component connects and how force enters the eye. Include the pin, supporting parts and expected movement. A flat drilled lug, a fork and a closed forged ring create different interfaces even when each is casually called an eye bolt.

Show the articulation and load direction

Provide the range of movement and surrounding clearances. Identify whether the connection sees aligned tension, angular loading or changing directions. These details help the responsible engineer assess the load path and select the dimensions that require control.

Working on this type of part? Explore our custom eye & articulating bolts and include the functional requirements in your RFQ.

Treat lifting requirements explicitly

A custom ring geometry is not a working-load rating. Lifting-related use requires an approved design basis, suitable material condition and the specified verification and documentation. Do not infer a rating from dimensions, appearance or similarity to an unrelated catalog component.

Prepare a complete manufacturing review

Dimension the eye, shank transitions, thread and seating faces. State the required properties and acceptance checks. The forming and machining sequence should be considered with the function, rather than selecting a production method before the application requirements are understood.

Specification example

For a pivoting fixture connection, provide the mating clevis and pin. For a lifting requirement, include the approved lifting specification instead of using the fixture drawing as a substitute.

RFQ checklist

  • Linkage or lifting use
  • Mating pin and movement envelope
  • Load directions and design requirements
  • Material and final condition
  • Required verification and records

How to dimension a custom U-bolt

Inside width, bend shape and leg alignment determine whether a U-bolt fits the supported component. A clear drawing separates those features from the threaded connection.

By Theo Wan • ZUFEK Technical Editorial • Published October 29, 2026
IN THIS GUIDEIdentify the component being clampedDimension from consistent referencesReview bending and the material conditionInclude the rest of the joint
RELATED PRODUCTCustom U-Bolts ↗

Identify the component being clamped

Provide the pipe or frame cross-section and any saddle or liner. State whether contact is intended along a radius or against flat faces. The nominal outside size may not describe corner radii, coatings or protective layers that affect the actual fit.

Dimension from consistent references

Show inside width, bend radius or profile, leg length and threaded length using clear references. Avoid mixing outside and inside dimensions without defining the rod section. Include leg parallelism or position requirements when they affect installation into a bracket or plate.

Working on this type of part? Explore our custom u-bolts and include the functional requirements in your RFQ.

Review bending and the material condition

The selected grade, section and final condition affect how the bend is produced and verified. Specify mechanical and surface requirements instead of assuming any rod can be bent to the same shape without consequences. Manufacturing feasibility must be confirmed for the actual geometry.

Include the rest of the joint

Nuts, washers, saddles and supporting plates form the complete connection. Identify required engagement and any assembly restrictions. Agree the finished coating and a useful fit check so production inspection evaluates the part in the condition that will be supplied.

Specification example

If the U-bolt passes through two holes in a plate, supply the hole spacing and clearance. A correct bend profile alone does not guarantee that both threaded legs will enter the plate.

RFQ checklist

  • Clamped cross-section and liner
  • Inside width and bend profile
  • Leg length and alignment
  • Threaded engagement
  • Material, finish and fit check

Custom carriage bolts: specifying the square neck

The square neck is the functional anti-rotation feature of a carriage bolt. It should be matched to the mating hole and supporting material rather than treated as a cosmetic detail.

By Theo Wan • ZUFEK Technical Editorial • Published October 29, 2026
IN THIS GUIDEDefine the mating holeControl neck depth and transitionReview the domed head and bearing faceAgree the finished fit
RELATED PRODUCTCustom Carriage Bolts ↗

Define the mating hole

Provide hole shape, dimensions, corner condition and panel thickness. Explain whether the neck is intended to enter freely or engage during installation. The behavior depends on both the neck and the surrounding material, not simply the width across flats.

Control neck depth and transition

Specify square-neck length and its relationship to the head underside. Show transitions that affect seating in the panel. A neck that is too long for the stack can interfere with the nut-side assembly even when the head and thread dimensions are correct.

Working on this type of part? Explore our custom carriage bolts and include the functional requirements in your RFQ.

Review the domed head and bearing face

Head diameter and height affect appearance, clearance and the supporting footprint. Identify visible surfaces and any finish requirements. A smooth dome does not define the underside contact, so include the seating details that matter to the connection.

Agree the finished fit

Forming variation, coating and hole condition can influence assembly. Inspect the neck in the supplied finish and define any functional fit or anti-rotation check. Do not use a visual comparison with a standard carriage bolt as the only acceptance method for a custom neck.

Specification example

When adapting a carriage bolt to a thinner panel, review neck depth and the full clamp stack. Changing only the thread length may leave the actual seating problem unresolved.

RFQ checklist

  • Mating square hole and panel thickness
  • Neck width and depth
  • Under-head transitions
  • Finished head envelope
  • Fit and anti-rotation acceptance

Eccentric screw drawings: making the offset unambiguous

An eccentric feature needs a clear reference axis. Without a datum scheme, two manufacturers can interpret an apparently simple offset drawing differently.

By Theo Wan • ZUFEK Technical Editorial • Published October 29, 2026
IN THIS GUIDEIdentify the functional axisDefine offset and angular orientationDescribe the mating contactChoose an inspection setup that follows function
RELATED PRODUCTEccentric & Angled Head Screws ↗

Identify the functional axis

Show which shank, shoulder or thread establishes the assembly reference. Dimension the eccentric feature relative to that reference rather than an arbitrary drawing edge. If the thread does not locate the part in service, explain which smooth feature actually does.

Define offset and angular orientation

Specify the amount of eccentricity and any required orientation to a slot, flat or drive. An offset without angular control may be acceptable for one adjuster and unsuitable for another. Include the intended adjustment positions and how they will be identified during assembly.

Working on this type of part? Explore our eccentric & angled head screws and include the functional requirements in your RFQ.

Describe the mating contact

Provide the follower, bore or surface moved by the eccentric feature. Show clearances and travel limits. The assembly determines whether a geometric change produces the desired adjustment; the screw drawing alone cannot establish the motion of every connected component.

Choose an inspection setup that follows function

The inspection plan should establish the same reference features used in the design. Discuss the practical measurement of offset, form and orientation before production. A photograph can illustrate the concept but is not an adequate substitute for controlled datum and dimensional requirements.

Specification example

For a camera-module adjuster, show the feature that contacts the module and the surface that locates the screw. This helps distinguish the adjustment geometry from incidental machining surfaces.

RFQ checklist

  • Functional locating axis
  • Offset and orientation
  • Mating contact and travel
  • Critical datum relationships
  • Agreed measurement setup

DESIGN & DIMENSIONS / 2 MIN READ

Double-ended studs: preventing mixed-thread assembly errors

Different threads at the two ends can solve an interface problem and create an identification problem. The drawing, inspection plan and packaging should distinguish each end clearly.

By Theo Wan • ZUFEK Technical Editorial • Published October 29, 2026
IN THIS GUIDESpecify the two ends independentlyExplain the center sectionPlan identification before packingGauge and review both interfaces
RELATED PRODUCTCustom Double-Ended Studs ↗

Specify the two ends independently

Provide diameter, pitch, handedness, fit and usable length for each threaded end. Do not assume a repeated note applies to both ends if the interfaces differ. Show any thread runout or relief that affects seating against the center section.

Explain the center section

A plain shank, shoulder or wrench flat can serve a locating or assembly function. Dimension its axial relationship to both threads. Clarify whether a face should seat against a mating part or whether the stud is installed to a separate depth requirement.

Working on this type of part? Explore our custom double-ended studs and include the functional requirements in your RFQ.

Plan identification before packing

If the ends look similar, discuss permitted marks, packaging orientation or another agreed distinction. Avoid an unapproved color or permanent mark on a functional surface. Identification requirements should appear in the order documentation so repeat batches use the same method.

Gauge and review both interfaces

Each end needs the appropriate acceptance method for its own specification. Inspection records should identify the end being checked, especially when the same nominal diameter uses different pitches. A successful trial in one mating part does not establish the other end conforms.

Specification example

For a stud joining two different thread sizes, label the ends A and B on the drawing and use the same labels in the inspection plan. Keep that convention on sample reports and packaging instructions.

RFQ checklist

  • Complete specification for both threads
  • Center-section dimensions
  • Installation sequence and seating
  • Approved end identification
  • Separate thread acceptance checks

DESIGN & DIMENSIONS / 2 MIN READ

Reduced-shank screws: why transitions need attention

A narrow center section changes the geometry of a threaded connection. Its purpose and transition details must be defined before the manufacturing route is selected.

By Theo Wan • ZUFEK Technical Editorial • Published October 29, 2026
IN THIS GUIDEState the purpose of the reduced sectionDimension the whole transitionReview properties with the responsible engineerInspect the supplied condition
RELATED PRODUCTReduced & Variable Shank Screws ↗

State the purpose of the reduced section

Explain whether the waist provides clearance, a specified compliance characteristic or another design function. These are different requirements. A visually similar reduction can perform differently when the section length, material condition or surrounding joint changes.

Dimension the whole transition

Include the minimum diameter, axial length and transition radii or reliefs. Identify functional surfaces and features that may be blended. Leaving a transition to general workshop practice can create variation where the designer expected a consistent section and load path.

Working on this type of part? Explore our reduced & variable shank screws and include the functional requirements in your RFQ.

Review properties with the responsible engineer

For a clearance-driven design, provide the interfering component envelope. If the reduced section has a mechanical function, include the approved engineering requirements separately from the clearance drawing.
