Centering, contact and sealing are distinct functions. Identify the intended contact surface and the motion or loading involved. A conical shape does not itself demonstrate sealing performance or establish the location of a connected assembly.

Use a complete dimensional definition

Specify angle or taper ratio with the necessary diameters and axial references. Make it clear where the taper begins and ends. Avoid redundant or conflicting dimensions that imply different surfaces when interpreted at the manufacturing or inspection stage.

For a locating cone, provide the corresponding seat and insertion limit. For a sealing design, also provide the sealing arrangement and required test rather than relying on a generic taper note.

For a screw with a pin under its flange, provide the hole pattern and the flange seating face. These details allow the pin location to be evaluated in the same assembly condition in which it will operate.

A collection of individual lengths does not always establish the functional stack. Agree measurement references and checks for the distances that matter. Include final coating and treatment conditions when they can affect the supplied diameters or seating surfaces.

Specification example

For two bearings separated by a shoulder, identify the bearing seating faces and the required spacing between them. This is more useful than applying the same tight tolerance to every unrelated axial dimension.

  • Functional locating shoulders
  • Datum-based axial dimensions

Specify panel material, thickness, hardness where required and any finish present during installation. Include local geometry and access for the press tooling. These conditions influence how the sheet engages the retention features and how the finished connection can be verified.

Define the hole and retention geometry

Show hole dimensions, preparation and permitted edge condition. Define the stud undercut, serrations or other press-in features on the approved drawing. A resemblance to a standard proprietary part does not establish that the custom version has the same installation requirements or ratings.

Working on this type of part? Explore our custom clinch screws & studs and include the functional requirements in your RFQ.

For a custom stud in a coated panel, state whether coating occurs before or after installation. That sequence can change the fit and the inspection conditions and should be resolved before production.

  • Stud retention features

Define the thread before the production method

Provide designation, profile, pitch, tolerance class and usable engagement. Include special roots, crests or transitions where applicable. A request to roll the thread does not resolve an incomplete thread specification, and a generic thread name may not define a custom profile.

Review material and the proposed sequence

Rolling displaces material; cutting removes material. Their feasibility depends on the grade, condition, geometry and available tooling. Discuss the sequence relative to heat treatment and other finishing operations rather than assuming the same process can be transferred unchanged to a different material.

Working on this type of part? Explore our special & compound thread profiles and include the functional requirements in your RFQ.

Rolling may provide useful surface and material effects in suitable conditions, but the finished connection still needs the specified properties and acceptance. State the required gauging, dimensional checks and any profile verification. Inspection should evaluate the final supplied condition, including coating where relevant. If a manufacturing method is mandatory, record it explicitly and explain any approval requirement for a proposed route change.

Specification example

For a short run of a special trapezoidal thread, provide the complete profile and mating requirement. Ask the supplier to explain the proposed route instead of selecting a process solely from a general cost comparison.

  • Complete thread geometry
  • Material and final condition
  • Treatment and threading sequence
  • Mandatory versus preferred method
  • Final thread acceptance

For a transverse pin hole through a hollow screw, show the internal intersection and describe how the pin is inserted. This gives the manufacturer a concrete edge condition to review before quoting.

RELATED PRODUCTHollow & Through-Hole Screws ↗

Describe the contamination concern

Explain whether particles could block a passage, damage a contact surface or affect another assembly function. Identify internal bores, thread roots and other areas that matter. A generic clean-and-dry instruction does not communicate a particle limit or a verified extraction method.

Agree the method and acceptance criteria

If a recognized cleanliness framework is required, specify the applicable procedure and project criteria. State the surfaces, extraction approach, reporting and acceptance limits relevant to the part. A standard number by itself does not define all of these choices for a particular order.

Working on this type of part? Explore our hollow & through-hole screws and include the functional requirements in your RFQ.

Separate deburring from cleaning

Attached burrs and loose residue are different conditions. The manufacturing route should address edge condition before the agreed cleaning process. Inspection may need to evaluate both, especially at cross holes and internal intersections where visual access is limited.

Protect the result through handling

Define drying, handling and packaging appropriate to the requirement. Recontamination can occur after cleaning if the process and packing sequence are not coordinated. Include the expected condition at delivery and any restrictions on protective oil or other residues.

Specification example

For an adhesive-dispensing passage, provide the smallest relevant flow section and the contamination acceptance requirement. A cleaning process can then be reviewed against the actual passage rather than a general appearance target.

  • Functional contamination concern
  • Specified surfaces and passages
  • Extraction and acceptance method
  • Permitted residues and dryness
  • Handling and packaging controls

What CCD vision inspection can check on a custom screw

Camera-based dimensional inspection can evaluate visible features of a screw, but the image, setup and inspection program must match the requirement. It is one part of a complete acceptance plan.

By Theo Wan • ZUFEK Technical Editorial • Published October 29, 2026
IN THIS GUIDEChoose the visible features to measureReview presentation and lightingRecognize what the image does not establishValidate and maintain the inspection programValidate presentation and edge visibilityDefine coverage and reject handlingPair optical checks with the missing methods
RELATED PRODUCTShoulder & Step Screws ↗

Choose the visible features to measure

Overall length, head diameter and stepped external profiles can be useful targets for optical checks when they are presented clearly. Identify the actual drawing characteristics rather than requesting a generic camera inspection with no defined measurements or acceptance limits.

Review presentation and lighting

Stable support, suitable optics and controlled lighting help produce consistent edges. Backlighting is useful for silhouette-based checks, while other surface features may require a different lighting arrangement. Establish the inspection view for the part rather than assuming one image reveals every characteristic.

Working on this type of part? Explore our shoulder & step screws and include the functional requirements in your RFQ.

Recognize what the image does not establish

A visible outline does not prove material grade, hardness or internal features hidden from the camera. Thread functional acceptance may require the specified gauges or other methods. The inspection plan should identify complementary checks instead of presenting one camera station as complete evidence of every requirement.

Validate and maintain the inspection program

Agree the measurement setup, acceptance limits, reference parts and any checks used to confirm consistent operation. Document changes to part revision or finish that may affect the image. Inspection coverage and handling of rejected parts should be defined for the actual order.

Validate presentation and edge visibility

Review part orientation, lighting, contrast and focus for each intended characteristic. Compare the programmed result with a suitable reference measurement using representative parts. Do not transfer a setup unchanged to a different coating, shape or presentation without checking whether the relevant edge is still detected appropriately.

Define coverage and reject handling

Document which external features the system evaluates and which are outside the validated program. Agree how borderline and rejected parts are handled, how setup changes are controlled and what record is retained. A pass indication is evidence only for the characteristics and conditions actually evaluated, not for every requirement on the drawing.

Pair optical checks with the missing methods

Use appropriate complementary checks for internal passages, thread acceptance, surface texture and material properties. A silhouette may show part of a thread outline without establishing the complete thread fit. Mitutoyo’s vision-measurement guide describes optical edge detection and alignment; the production inspection plan must still establish applicability to the actual screw.

Specification example

For a shoulder screw, define head diameter, shoulder length and overall length as separate checks. Then specify how the thread and any internal drive requirements are verified outside that silhouette measurement.

RFQ checklist

  • Drawing characteristics and limits
  • Required views and presentation
  • Calibration and reference checks
  • Complementary gauges or tests
  • Coverage and reject-handling plan

Link the sample to a controlled specification

Record drawing number, revision, material condition and finish. Identify any agreed deviations separately. A loose sample with no revision history can create confusion if it is later used as a master for a repeat order or a manufacturing change.

Define the evidence before making parts

Agree which dimensions, material documents, process records and functional checks are required. The sample plan should follow the actual risk and acceptance requirements. Waiting until parts arrive to request additional tests can delay approval or require another manufacturing batch.

Working on this type of part? Explore our custom metal screws and include the functional requirements in your RFQ.

Separate visual and functional approval

Appearance, tool fit and trial assembly can reveal useful information, but they do not replace all drawing checks. Record what each review establishes and who accepts it. If a mating fixture is used, identify its revision and relevant condition as part of the approval record.

Close the feedback loop

Document changes arising from the review and decide whether they require a new drawing revision or another sample. Preserve an approved reference only with a clear record of what it controls. Production release should refer to the final agreed specification rather than an informal message chain.

Specification example

If a trial assembly leads to a longer shoulder, revise the drawing and identify the replacement sample. Keeping the original sample as an unexplained master can reintroduce the superseded dimension on a later order.

  • Required dimensional report
  • Material and process evidence
  • Defined assembly or appearance checks
  • Recorded approval and change disposition

Classify the characteristics

Identify critical, functional and other drawing requirements through the responsible quality process. Explain the consequence of a nonconforming feature. This provides a basis for discussing which characteristics need screening and which can use the agreed sampling or approval method.

Define what full inspection means

Specify the feature, method and handling for every-piece screening. A camera check of length does not mean every thread, material property and internal surface has been verified. Destructive tests also cannot be applied to each delivered component in the same way as a non-destructive dimensional check.

Agree sampling as a documented plan

Inspection is more effective when supported by stable manufacturing and traceable records. Define reference checks, measurement capability and lot handling as appropriate. Additional inspection should address an identified requirement rather than simply adding a broad label that neither side can demonstrate.

Specification example

A buyer may request every-piece optical length screening while using separate thread-gauge sampling and material documentation. Writing each requirement explicitly is clearer than calling the entire order fully inspected.

  • Lot definition and sampling rules
  • Failure disposition

Document the tool method, acceptance criteria and any required checks with the approved part specification. If the screw or surface system changes, consider whether the assembly instruction needs review. The quotation should make clear which tests or reports are included and which require separate agreement.

Specification example

Replacing a plain screw with an integral flange changes the bearing interface. Review the joint assumptions before carrying over the original torque instruction solely because the nominal thread is unchanged.

If a prototype shoulder is finish-turned but production is proposed with grinding after treatment, review the final dimensions and surface acceptance. Approve the resulting part condition rather than only the process name.

Drawing revision control for repeat custom fastener orders

Repeat orders should repeat the approved specification, not the ambiguities of an old email. A small revision-control habit can prevent expensive confusion across drawings, samples and inspection records.

By Theo Wan • ZUFEK Technical Editorial • Published October 29, 2026
IN THIS GUIDEUse one identified production drawingDocument changes and deviations separatelyConnect records to the correct revisionConfirm the specification on reordering
RELATED PRODUCTCustom Metal Screws ↗

Use one identified production drawing

Include drawing number, revision and units in the RFQ and purchase documentation. Mark superseded files clearly within the agreed document process. A descriptive filename alone may not establish which issue was approved if several attachments circulate between engineering and purchasing.

Document changes and deviations separately

A permanent design change and a temporary accepted deviation are different decisions. Record the affected feature, quantity or lot and approval scope. Do not allow a sample concession to silently become the specification for every future order.

Working on this type of part? Explore our custom metal screws and include the functional requirements in your RFQ.

Connect records to the correct revision

Inspection reports, approved samples and packaging references should identify the applicable drawing. If a change affects the manufacturing or inspection route, review those documents too. Updating the drawing while retaining an obsolete inspection reference can leave the production team working to inconsistent requirements.

Confirm the specification on reordering

For a repeat purchase, state whether the previous drawing, finish and acceptance plan still apply. Identify any changes to mating parts or assembly conditions. A nominally unchanged screw can need review when the customer changes the component around it.

Specification example

A buyer reordering a part can include one line stating the approved drawing revision and inspection-plan issue. That is more reliable than asking for the same as last time when several sample versions exist.

RFQ checklist

  • Drawing number and revision
  • Permanent versus temporary changes
  • Linked sample and report references
  • Affected process documents
  • Repeat-order confirmation

Packaging and lot traceability for custom screw orders

Packaging is part of the delivered condition. It should protect functional surfaces, preserve identification and make the incoming inspection and assembly process practical.

By Theo Wan • ZUFEK Technical Editorial • Published October 29, 2026
IN THIS GUIDEIdentify what needs protectionDefine quantities and identificationCoordinate cleanliness and preservationConnect the lot to the records
RELATED PRODUCTCustom Metal Screws ↗

Identify what needs protection

Consider exposed threads, precision shoulders, applied locking material and any cleaned internal passage. State special protection requirements rather than assuming bulk packing is suitable for every part. The supplier needs to know which handling damage or contamination would make the component unacceptable.

Define quantities and identification

Agree pack quantity, part number, drawing revision and lot information required on the label. If similar products or mixed-thread ends are supplied, consider how the receiving team distinguishes them. Avoid introducing unapproved markings on the component itself to solve a packaging identification issue.

Working on this type of part? Explore our custom metal screws and include the functional requirements in your RFQ.

Coordinate cleanliness and preservation

Protective oil, corrosion prevention and clean packaging serve different needs and can conflict. Specify permitted residues and the expected condition at delivery. Packaging should follow the agreed cleaning and finishing sequence so it does not reintroduce contamination or damage a pre-applied feature.

Connect the lot to the records

Define which inspection or material documents accompany the shipment and how they relate to the identified lot. Keep the traceability requirement proportionate to the actual order. A label containing a batch number is only useful when the agreed records can be associated with that number.

Specification example

For two nearly identical shoulder lengths, use separate clearly labeled packages and the correct part references. A shared bulk bag can defeat otherwise careful dimensional inspection by creating an avoidable assembly mix-up.

RFQ checklist

  • Functional surfaces to protect
  • Pack quantity and separation
  • Part, revision and lot label
  • Permitted preservation materials
  • Linked shipment documents

OUR BACKGROUND

Since 2005, ZUFEK has focused on custom metal fasteners where a standard catalog part does not fully answer the drawing. Our work centers on the details that affect assembly: a locating shoulder, a special drive, a through bore, an unusual thread or several functional features combined in one component.

Our Dalang location places the business within Dongguan’s manufacturing community. We work with customers on drawing clarification, sample requirements and repeat production, keeping material, geometry, finish and acceptance requirements connected throughout the quotation process.

Our production capacity is on the order of several million parts per month. Actual output, order allocation and delivery timing depend on part complexity, material, tooling, secondary operations and the agreed inspection scope.

    正在加载邮件配置…

    TLS／证书高级设置

    始终校验证书有效期、主机名和信任链，不使用忽略证书错误的方式发送。587端口强制升级TLS。

    SMTP转接服务部署设置

    当前网站托管不能直连SMTP，需要在支持SMTP的服务器部署随项目提供的转接服务。未接通时可以保存SMTP信息，但不能启用发送，也不会显示为发送正常。

    转接服务必须由你控制，SMTP凭据会通过HTTPS发送给该服务。服务接收经认证的请求，并验证SMTP目标、TLS证书和发送幂等编号。部署包与说明位于项目smtp-bridge目录；需先部署到你控制的服务器。

    测试发送与诊断

    先保存配置，再验证；保存配置不代表已连接或已送达。

    当前保存的配置

    SMTP接受发送请求不保证最终投递到收件箱。请检查收件箱、垃圾邮件及邮件服务器日志，并配置SPF／DKIM／DMARC。测试与诊断每分钟最多执行一次，测试内容不含客户询盘资料。

    邮件失败不会删除已保存的询盘。启用后，已保存但未通知的询盘也会进入通知重试队列；访客自动确认仅针对启用后的新询盘。未配置独立调度前，重试由询盘提交或后台读取询盘触发，也可手动重试。转接服务尚未部署、账号未验证或收件未确认时，不能依赖邮件通知。

01

Drive options

Pin-in six-lobe, Y-type, five-lobe / pentalobe, two-hole spanner and triangular drives.

Tool interface

Define the actual drive profile, dimensions, pin position and tool clearance.

03

Head configurations

Review head diameter, height, access and any flange requirements.

Where this design fits

Equipment housings, security devices, charging equipment and service-access panels.

What to include in the RFQ

Provide the drive drawing or matching tool specification. Tamper resistance depends on tool availability and the complete assembly; it is not absolute security.

Common specification questions

Does a tamper-resistant drive guarantee security?

Can a special drive be combined with a flange or shoulder?

Follow a complete application design

Review the enclosure service-drive concept ↗

Match the drive to the installed tool access

  1. Drive and bit: identify the actual profile, engagement depth and, for a pin-in drive, the pin and matching bit clearance.
  2. Access envelope: show the tool approach, neighboring walls and the space needed to insert and withdraw the tool.
  3. Service trial: check installation and authorized removal with the representative housing and matching tool.

Keep drive acceptance and access acceptance separate. A pin-in profile can restrict casual access, but the profile alone does not establish a security rating.

Specify the drive, not just its name

Supply a controlled drawing or matching tool specification, including recess depth, center-pin geometry and tolerances. Review service access in the installed housing

A security screw may be easy to drive on a bench but inaccessible inside a recessed enclosure. Include the housing recess, tool approach, driver diameter and permitted insertion depth. An enlarged flange can also interfere with a nearby wall. Review the assembled condition before fixing the head envelope, especially when a restricted drive is combined with a non-standard head.

Balance deterrence with maintenance

A special drive discourages casual removal; it does not provide an absolute security rating. Decide who needs service access and how replacement tools will be controlled. Consider whether the screw must remain captive when a panel is opened. These decisions affect the assembly and purchasing specification, rather than being solved by the drive recess alone.

Approve the production tool interface

Evaluate the intended driver with representative finished samples. Check engagement, seating and the agreed assembly behavior after any coating. Can CCD inspect the complete bore?

Are hollow screws pressure-rated?

Follow the smallest wall and the hidden bore edge

Common specification questions

Which point is best for a shaft?

The answer depends on the shaft surface, permitted marking and whether the point clamps or locates. Supply the mating geometry and functional requirement.

Can holding force be specified from screw size alone?

No. Engagement, contact, material, assembly and loading affect the complete connection. The responsible design must establish the requirement.

Choose the point by its contact with the mating part

The point form determines how contact is made. Select it with the mating surface, adjustment frequency and allowable marking, then define usable thread and tool access.

  1. Flat point: define the mating face and agree the permitted contact marks.
  2. Cone point: show the intended recess or permitted indentation and the location it must engage.
  3. Dog point: define the projection and mating hole or slot; check both clearance and available depth.
  4. Cup point: review rim contact and any indentation against the permissible damage to the mating surface.

Review repeated adjustment and retention on the actual joint. Point geometry and screw diameter alone do not provide a universal holding-force or tightening-torque value.

Compare the four point forms and selection worksheet ↗

Choose the point around the mating surface

Cone, cup, flat and dog points serve different contact arrangements. A locating dog point needs its mating recess defined. A point that bites into a shaft may leave a mark that is unacceptable elsewhere. State whether the screw locates, clamps or acts as a stop, and show the surface it contacts before selecting the tip.

Keep engagement and access visible

A headless screw can sit below or project above the mating surface. Show the installed position, available tool depth and required thread engagement. A longer screw is not automatically a stronger connection if the actual engaged length is unchanged. Recess geometry, material condition and the mating tapped part all belong in the review.

Distinguish retention from fine adjustment

A set screw used as a shaft retainer has a different acceptance question from one used as a fine positioning stop. For a stop, define the contact end, adjustment travel and locking method. For retention, define the assembled functional requirement with the responsible designer; do not assign a universal holding force from the screw size alone.

Inspect the features that establish the function

Verify thread acceptance, tip form, overall length and the specified material condition. An external vision profile cannot by itself validate the socket or assembled holding behavior. Reduced & Variable Shank Screws

A reduced or stepped shank introduces a deliberate change in section between functional features.

Discuss this custom part ↗
DRAWING-DEFINED FEATURES
01

Section change

Specify minimum diameter, transition radii and axial lengths.

02

Functional intent

Explain whether the feature provides clearance, compliance or another assembly function.

03

Mechanical verification

Review stress concentration and required testing for the actual load.

Where this design fits

Custom flexible joints, clearance-controlled assemblies and engineered threaded connections.

What to include in the RFQ

A reduced shank does not automatically prevent cracking. Supply load and fatigue requirements for design review.

Carbon steel, 10B21, SUS304/316, aluminum, copper/brass and titanium alloy requirements can be discussed. Suitability is specific to the part, grade and process.

Transitions and minimum section

Dimension the reduced section and both transitions relative to the functional surfaces. Explain whether it provides clearance, a particular elastic behavior or an assembly feature. A smaller shank changes the load path; geometry alone cannot substantiate a fatigue or stress-reduction claim without the relevant design assessment.

Review the route before fixing the quotation

For reduced & variable shank screws, review Swiss-Type & CNC Turning, Cold Heading + Secondary Machining, CCD Vision & Dimensional Inspection against the drawing and quantity. Identify which features can be produced in the initial shape and which require a separate setup. A change to a functional shoulder, bore, drive or thread can change the proposed route as well as the inspection effort.

The drawing review should resolve section change; functional intent; mechanical verification. Keep material condition and finishing allowance attached to those requirements. Define the acceptance condition for critical features and approve any proposed dimensional change before comparing samples with the original assembly.

From drawing to approved samples

A reduced shank does not automatically prevent cracking. Supply load and fatigue requirements for design review. Identify the drawing revision, prototype quantity and expected repeat demand. Where the first part is based on an existing sample, separately confirm material and hidden features rather than inferring them from appearance.

The typical sampling lead time, including tooling, is approximately 10–15 days. The schedule is confirmed after drawing review and agreement on the sample specification; material availability, special treatment and inspection requirements can affect the confirmed date. Confirm when the agreed schedule starts in the quotation. Sample approval and repeat-production delivery are separate milestones.

Provide the panel specification and acceptance tests. Do not assume a custom feature shares the ratings of a branded standard clinch part. Identify the drawing revision, prototype quantity and expected repeat demand. Where the first part is based on an existing sample, separately confirm material and hidden features rather than inferring them from appearance.

The typical sampling lead time, including tooling, is approximately 10–15 days. The schedule is confirmed after drawing review and agreement on the sample specification; material availability, special treatment and inspection requirements can affect the confirmed date. Confirm when the agreed schedule starts in the quotation. Sample approval and repeat-production delivery are separate milestones.

ROUTE 01 / FORMING

Multi-Station Cold Heading

Wire is cut and formed through a sequence of dies. Head, flange and some shoulder features can be integrated into a repeatable production route.

MANUFACTURING CAPABILITIESDrawing review exampleMulti-Station Cold HeadingSwiss-Type & CNC TurningHot Heading & ForgingCold Heading + Secondary MachiningThread Rolling, Cutting & TappingSecondary & Precision OperationsMaterial-Specific Heat TreatmentCoatings & Surface TreatmentsCleaning, Locking & AssemblyCCD Vision & Dimensional InspectionComplete route examples ↗

Where it fits

Repeated screw geometries and production volumes that justify dedicated tooling. Head volume, material formability and extrusion limits guide the die sequence.

Operations to review

Cut-off, preforming, heading, extrusion, local reduction and pre-piercing. Deep bores, side features and complex undercuts may require later machining.

What drives the quotation

Tooling investment, batch quantity, material, head-to-shank ratios and the secondary operations that remain. Cold heading is not automatically the cheapest route at every volume.

Mechanical considerations

Cold forming can provide favorable grain flow and work hardening. Final properties still depend on material, deformation, heat treatment and verified acceptance requirements.

Prepare a complete specification

Use the RFQ checklist, review materials and include the required inspection and documentation.

Drawing review example

Cold heading a flanged screw with a deep drive

Illustrative drawing review. Confirm the route, dimensions and acceptance for your part.

What drives the route
Review the head and recess together in section. Enlarging the flange changes the metal volume to be moved, while a deeper drive leaves less material below the recess. Identify the under-head transition and usable bearing face before splitting the blank into forming stages.
What changes the quotation
Separate the cost of heading tools from recurring pieces and any later recess, shoulder or hole machining. Ask which revision changes would require a tool change and whether the proposed wire condition and batch size support the formed route.
How to release the sample
Use samples from the intended forming route. Confirm the recess fit, flange seating and under-head geometry on the finished part, and agree what forming defects are unacceptable and how they will be checked. A turned mock-up can prove assembly access without proving formed-head quality.

ROUTE 02 / BAR MACHINING

Swiss-Type & CNC Turning

Bar-fed turning and turn-mill operations create drawing-specific steps, bores and other details with flexible programming.

MANUFACTURING CAPABILITIESDrawing review exampleMulti-Station Cold HeadingSwiss-Type & CNC TurningHot Heading & ForgingCold Heading + Secondary MachiningThread Rolling, Cutting & TappingSecondary & Precision OperationsMaterial-Specific Heat TreatmentCoatings & Surface TreatmentsCleaning, Locking & AssemblyCCD Vision & Dimensional InspectionComplete route examples ↗

Where it fits

Prototypes, varied geometries, small batches and parts with several machined features. Actual batch economics depend on cycle time, stock and setup.

Swiss-type and fixed-head choices

Part length-to-diameter ratio, support and the required operations guide the choice. Turn-mill capability can combine turning, flats, holes and tapped features where the machine setup permits.

Design inputs

Provide bore depth, wall thickness, datum relationships, burr limits and surface finish. Access, tool reach and workholding remain feasibility constraints.

Cost and properties

Material removal increases chip generation and may increase unit cost. A machined part is not universally weaker than a formed part: grade, geometry, heat treatment and loading determine performance.

Prepare a complete specification

Use the RFQ checklist, review materials and include the required inspection and documentation.

Drawing review example

Check the remaining wall before quoting a hollow screw

Illustrative drawing review. Confirm the route, dimensions and acceptance for your part.

What drives the route
Illustrative section only: an outside diameter of at least 7.96 mm and a bore of at most 4.04 mm leave 1.96 mm radial wall if concentric. With up to 0.15 mm centre offset at that section, the minimum wall is (7.96 − 4.04) ÷ 2 − 0.15 = 1.81 mm. This simple circular check excludes threads, cross-holes and local transitions.
What changes the quotation
Identify the minimum wall and bore axis where they matter, rather than only giving nominal diameters. A long bore, interrupted cut, tighter position requirement or second workholding setup can change cycle time, tool access and the inspection method.
How to release the sample
Check bore and outer geometry in the agreed datums and after release from the fixture. Separately verify hole intersections and burrs where a cable or fluid passes. The section calculation is a geometry check, not a pressure or load rating.

Hot Heading & Forging

Where it fits

Large heads, eye forms and substantial sections may suit hot forging. There is no universal M24 changeover; material, equipment and shape determine the practical route.

Typical follow-up work

Trimming, scale removal, machining of seating faces or holes, threading and the specified heat treatment.

Separate the forged eye blank from the finished load path

Cold Heading + Secondary Machining

Why combine processes

Integrate repeated bulk geometry through forming, then machine the features that need a different tool path or control. Tooling and machining must be evaluated together.

Typical feature split

Head and rough shank by forming; shoulder finish, reliefs, flats or side holes by secondary operations. The exact split follows feasibility review.

PROCESS / THREAD GENERATION

Thread Rolling, Cutting & Tapping

The thread profile, material and batch conditions determine whether rolling, cutting, grinding or an internal tapping process is appropriate.

MANUFACTURING CAPABILITIESDrawing review exampleMulti-Station Cold HeadingSwiss-Type & CNC TurningHot Heading & ForgingCold Heading + Secondary MachiningThread Rolling, Cutting & TappingSecondary & Precision OperationsMaterial-Specific Heat TreatmentCoatings & Surface TreatmentsCleaning, Locking & AssemblyCCD Vision & Dimensional InspectionComplete route examples ↗

Flat-die and cylindrical-die rolling

External threads are formed by displacement. Suitable material condition, blank diameter and tool geometry are essential. Machine capability sets the actual size range; no universal M0.8–M12 limit applies.

Single-point cutting and special profiles

Turning can address specified pitches, tapers and special profiles where tooling and access permit. NPT, MJ and other named threads require the applicable complete specification, not an approximate profile.

Internal cut and form tapping

Cut tapping removes material; form tapping displaces a sufficiently ductile material and needs the correct pre-hole. Neither method is universally stronger in every grade and geometry.

Acceptance and sequence

Define designation, class, usable length, runout and gauging. Rolling may improve fatigue behavior in suitable conditions, but is not a blanket strength guarantee. Review whether threading occurs before or after heat treatment.

Prepare a complete specification

Use the RFQ checklist, review materials and include the required inspection and documentation.

Drawing review example

A gauge pass does not establish usable engagement

Illustrative drawing review. Confirm the route, dimensions and acceptance for your part.

Secondary & Precision Operations

Drilling, reaming and milling

Axial bores, radial holes, pin holes, flats, squares, drive recesses and local slots. Define position, edge breaks, hole exits and access.

Knurling, grooves and tip work

Eccentric, angled and press operations

Control the hidden edge of an intersecting hole

PROCESS / MATERIAL CONDITION

Material-Specific Heat Treatment

Heat-treatment selection follows the alloy, required condition and applicable acceptance specification. One sequence cannot be applied to every screw.

MANUFACTURING CAPABILITIESDrawing review exampleMulti-Station Cold HeadingSwiss-Type & CNC TurningHot Heading & ForgingCold Heading + Secondary MachiningThread Rolling, Cutting & TappingSecondary & Precision OperationsMaterial-Specific Heat TreatmentCoatings & Surface TreatmentsCleaning, Locking & AssemblyCCD Vision & Dimensional InspectionComplete route examples ↗

Quench and temper

Suitable carbon and alloy steels can be processed to specified mechanical requirements. Property classes such as 8.8, 10.9 and 12.9 require an applicable specification and verification; treatment names alone do not establish the class.

Case hardening and boron steel

Carburizing and hardening can produce a hardened surface with a different core condition. A grade such as 10B21 does not by itself prescribe carburizing: specify core properties, case requirements and application.

Stainless and titanium distinctions

304/316 austenitic stainless steels are not precipitation-hardening grades. Solution annealing serves a different purpose from aging 17-4PH. Titanium and other alloys need grade-specific treatment; do not transfer a stainless cycle to them.

Stress relief and stability

Stress-relief or specialist cryogenic treatments are selected only where justified by material condition and dimensional needs. State the required final condition and review distortion, corrosion and finish compatibility.

Technical references

  • BSSA: stainless steel families
  • Carpenter: 17-4PH material data

Use the RFQ checklist, review materials and include the required inspection and documentation.

Specify a wear surface and a tough core separately

What drives the route
For a steel stop or tapping feature, identify the working surface and the core requirement. If the design needs a hardened case, define the depth criterion, test method and location. Do not substitute surface hardness for core properties or use a steel treatment note on a stainless or titanium grade.
What changes the quotation
Decide which dimensions are established before and after treatment. A precision shoulder may need finishing stock and a different inspection sequence; special case requirements or destructive checks can affect treatment lot size and turnaround.
How to release the sample
Tie the agreed hardness or case evidence to the treatment lot. Check the final geometry after finishing and confirm that any stock removal is consistent with the required surface condition. If a finished property class is ordered, verify it by its applicable acceptance basis.

PROCESS / SURFACE SYSTEM

Coatings & Surface Treatments

Specify a complete surface system: substrate condition, coating, thickness, functional surfaces and acceptance criteria.

MANUFACTURING CAPABILITIESDrawing review exampleMulti-Station Cold HeadingSwiss-Type & CNC TurningHot Heading & ForgingCold Heading + Secondary MachiningThread Rolling, Cutting & TappingSecondary & Precision OperationsMaterial-Specific Heat TreatmentCoatings & Surface TreatmentsCleaning, Locking & AssemblyCCD Vision & Dimensional InspectionComplete route examples ↗

Electroplated finishes

Zinc, colored or black zinc systems, bright/black nickel and zinc-nickel are discussion options. Name the actual coating specification, thickness and any friction or corrosion-test requirement. Cadmium is a restricted specialist option requiring project-specific review, not a default finish.

Zinc-flake and conversion systems

Zinc-flake systems, including Dacromet- or Geomet-type requirements, need an exact specification and applicability review. Black oxide and passivation depend on the substrate. Non-electrolytic deposition does not remove every possible hydrogen source from the full process.

Organic and vacuum coatings

Electrophoretic coating, PTFE-based coatings, powder/paint and PVD can address selected friction, appearance or surface functions. Thickness, cure temperature and thread fit need review.

High-strength fastener review

High-strength or high-hardness steels may be susceptible to hydrogen embrittlement from cleaning, pickling or plating. Baking and process controls can reduce risk but cannot guarantee its elimination. Select the coating and relief requirements under the applicable specification; neither a blanket zinc ban nor a blanket bake rule is sufficient.

Technical references

  • Würth: hydrogen embrittlement
  • Fastenal: embrittlement guidance

Use the RFQ checklist, review materials and include the required inspection and documentation.

Budget coating thickness at a smooth locating shoulder

Identify the coating system, substrate condition, covered or masked surfaces, thickness locations and any friction or corrosion requirement. Include pretreatment and relevant hydrogen-risk controls in the route; a finish name or colour does not define this scope.

Agree how thickness and coverage are checked, then verify final shoulder fit and thread acceptance separately. Where the assembly relies on controlled friction, require the appropriate evidence for the specified mating and tightening conditions, not only an appearance or salt-spray result.

PROCESS / FINAL CONDITION

Cleaning, Locking & Assembly

Cleanliness, burr control and pre-applied features are part of the finished-part specification, not an afterthought.

MANUFACTURING CAPABILITIESDrawing review exampleMulti-Station Cold HeadingSwiss-Type & CNC TurningHot Heading & ForgingCold Heading + Secondary MachiningThread Rolling, Cutting & TappingSecondary & Precision OperationsMaterial-Specific Heat TreatmentCoatings & Surface TreatmentsCleaning, Locking & AssemblyCCD Vision & Dimensional InspectionComplete route examples ↗

Cleaning and burr control

Degreasing, ultrasonic or suitable solvent cleaning, deburring, vibratory finishing and polishing are selected for the material and feature access. Define internal-bore and thread burr limits explicitly.

Technical cleanliness

If VDA 19 or ISO 16232 is specified, agree the applicable method, extraction, particle limits and reporting. Mentioning the standard alone does not define the acceptance level.

Pre-applied locking systems

Nylon patches and adhesive-based locking systems have different mechanisms. Specify the system, coverage, assembly conditions, reuse needs and required torque behavior.

Pre-assembly and sorting

Washers, O-rings, PTFE washers or springs may be included by drawing. Confirm sequence, retention and compatibility with heat/coating operations. Hydrogen-relief baking is applied where required by the selected material and finish specification.

Prepare a complete specification

Use the RFQ checklist, review materials and include the required inspection and documentation.

Drawing review example

Decide when to clean, apply locking patches and assemble seals

Illustrative drawing review. Confirm the route, dimensions and acceptance for your part.

What drives the route
For a captive screw with a seal or pre-applied patch, map every later cleaning, coating or heating step against compatibility. Identify the sealing face, required retention and patch position. Keep the passage and the useful thread clear of unintended residue.
What changes the quotation
Price the sequence as delivered: cleaning and drying, patch application or washer/seal assembly, sorting and packaging. Define cleanliness and any torque or reuse requirement by method and conditions rather than ordering a generic clean or locked part.
How to release the sample
Verify final condition after all operations and protective packing. Check retention, seal orientation and patch coverage separately from the agreed functional trial. Record the lot and distinguish technical-cleanliness results from any inspection of visible debris.

PROCESS / ACCEPTANCE

CCD Vision & Dimensional Inspection

Non-contact optical checks for screw length, head diameter and visible stepped profiles, combined with the gauges and tests required by the drawing.

MANUFACTURING CAPABILITIESDrawing review exampleMulti-Station Cold HeadingSwiss-Type & CNC TurningHot Heading & ForgingCold Heading + Secondary MachiningThread Rolling, Cutting & TappingSecondary & Precision OperationsMaterial-Specific Heat TreatmentCoatings & Surface TreatmentsCleaning, Locking & AssemblyCCD Vision & Dimensional InspectionComplete route examples ↗

CCD optical dimension checks

Camera-based vision measurement uses suitable optics, lighting and calibrated edge detection to check accessible external dimensions such as overall length, head diameter and shoulder profile. A stable presentation and validated inspection program are needed for the specified part.

Complementary verification

Silhouette inspection does not establish internal geometry, material strength or every thread characteristic. Use the specified thread gauges, additional dimensional methods and functional tests where required. Agree acceptance criteria and the actual inspection coverage.

Material and mechanical checks

Material documentation, HV/HRC hardness, tensile, torque or destructive testing are selected when applicable. A test name needs a method, sample quantity and acceptance criterion.

Surface and specialist checks

Coating thickness, specified salt-spray testing, metallography, fatigue and hydrogen-embrittlement evaluation require an agreed scope. Salt spray results do not directly predict service life.

Sampling versus full inspection

Agree which characteristics receive 100% screening, sampling or first-article approval. Equipment availability, external laboratory work and reporting are confirmed for the order; no unverified in-house laboratory claim is made.

Prepare a complete specification

Use the RFQ checklist, review materials and include the required inspection and documentation.

Drawing review example

Use CCD for visible dimensions, then cover the blind spots

Illustrative drawing review. Confirm the route, dimensions and acceptance for your part.

What drives the route
For a shoulder screw, identify the length and visible diameter or step that a stable, calibrated silhouette can evaluate. Present representative good, borderline and rejected samples at the expected orientations to verify the program. A view of the outline does not reveal the internal bore or material condition.
What changes the quotation
Separate the agreed optical screening characteristics from sampled thread, bore, hardness or coating checks. Agree the feature limits, reference method, sampling and records. A request for 100% screening needs a list of covered characteristics rather than a promise to measure everything.
How to release the sample
Compare results near the limits against the agreed reference, verify rejection handling, and record the drawing and program revision. Retain separate results for thread gauges, internal features and any material testing so a single pass flag is not mistaken for complete acceptance.

MATERIALS, STRENGTH & APPLICATIONS

Name the material.
Define its performance.

Compare grade, condition, strength and application needs. A material family alone does not determine the load capacity of a custom screw.

Read a material specification in three layers

Grade identifies the chemistry. Condition identifies the supplied or treated state. The finished-part requirement defines what the screw must meet after manufacturing. Keep all three in the drawing or purchase specification.

Compare numerical values only on the same basis: product form, section size, condition, test temperature and whether the value is nominal, typical or a specified minimum. A stock value cannot be used as an allowable joint load.

Use the grade table to build a shortlist, the processing checks to review feasibility, and the example request to prepare an RFQ. Proposed alternatives need an explicit approval against the same requirements.

Start with the job the material must do

Use the dominant requirement to choose a material family to investigate, then compare exact grades and conditions on its detail page. More than one family may remain suitable until the joint and environment are defined.

ILLUSTRATIVE PROCESS PLANNING

Three complete routes.
Defined by the drawing.

Use these examples to discuss the full chain. They are not fixed instructions: thread timing, heat treatment, grinding and coatings require material- and application-specific approval.

  7. Cleaning and specified coating system
  8. Hydrogen-relief operation where required by the process

Approve the route at the handoffs, not only at the end

Illustrative drawing review. Confirm the route, dimensions and acceptance for your part.

What drives the route
For a shoulder screw with a precision fit, identify the blank reference, which operation establishes the bearing shoulder, and which later treatment can move or build up that surface. Carry the same drawing revision and final-condition requirement across each handoff.
What changes the quotation
Compare each route to the same delivery scope: sample quantity, tooling, later operations, verification and records. Record which operations must be repeated or reapproved if the grade, finish, blank supplier or production method changes.
How to release the sample
Record the feature, operation that establishes it, verification stage and acceptance method. Link the approved sample and lot records to the route. For a change from turned samples to formed production, review each affected characteristic before approving repeat orders.

Decide the sequence before quoting.

Some threads are formed before heat treatment; other applications call for later thread generation. Final grinding and coating allowance must protect the specified fit. Hydrogen-relief baking belongs only where required and cannot be assumed for every zinc-flake or passivation route.

Sampling, tooling and production planning

Typical sampling lead time, including tooling, is approximately 10–15 days. The confirmed schedule follows drawing review and agreement on material, geometry, surface treatment and inspection requirements. Clarify the starting milestone in the quotation. Repeat-production delivery is quoted separately for the quantity and approved route.

Send a drawing revision, sample quantity, expected order volume and the intended application. Identify functional dimensions and required documents so the technical review can resolve the important details before tooling and sample approval.

Editorial approach

Published under an editorial pen name. Each guide focuses on information engineers and buyers can use to prepare drawings, compare manufacturing options and agree acceptance requirements.

Sources are linked where useful. Specification examples illustrate a discussion point and are not presented as customer case histories or test results.

A practical choice for drawing-defined fasteners where the required mechanical class, wear behavior and surface protection can be specified together.

Strength reference

Specify the finished fastener property class, not a strength inferred from the raw grade. Common nominal class references include 8.8, 10.9 and 12.9.

How to narrow the choice

For a machined locating part, start with the required wear surface and final condition. For a loaded fastening part, start with the finished mechanical requirements and applicable fastener standard; then review grade, section size, route and coating together.

Write an unambiguous material requirement

Include the designation standard, exact grade, product form, delivery condition, final mechanical requirements, surface treatment and acceptance evidence. Similar names across EN, ASTM, SAE, JIS or GB systems are comparison leads, not permission to substitute.

If the grade is not yet decided, send the load or locating function, environment, mating materials, quantity and drawing. Ask for a proposed grade and route with stated assumptions before approving the material.

The listed grades are comparisons for drawing review, not a declaration that every grade, size or treatment is held in stock. Availability, route and ordered evidence are confirmed in the quotation.

Selection, processing and acceptance

Choose the grade and condition together with the job the screw performs. The following checks connect the material shortlist to manufacturing and sample acceptance.

Function and grade choice
For a locating shoulder or stop, identify the contact surface, wear requirement and toughness needed at section changes. C45/C45E and 42CrMo4 are different starting choices; SAE 4140 needs its own stock specification. Choose from the final requirement rather than assuming that every alloy-steel part needs the highest property class.
Processing and final dimensions
Cold-heading wire and machining bar require different starting specifications. If hardening follows machining, plan the final sizing of shoulders and threads around distortion and coating build. For high-strength parts, review hydrogen-related process risk and the coating route; a later baking operation is not a universal guarantee against embrittlement.
What the sample must demonstrate
Keep the material heat identity, treatment batch and coating lot connected. Agree the applicable tensile, proof-load or hardness checks separately from dimensional inspection. For thin heads, hollow sections or reduced shanks, establish which finished-fastener tests apply and how the actual geometry is accepted.

Example: a machined shoulder with a heat-treated steel requirement

For a loaded bracket, keep the steel identity, material condition and finished screw requirements separate. Use the drawing to decide which properties are actually required at the shoulder and threaded section.

Illustrative material request. Drawing-specific limits and acceptance criteria remain to be agreed; this is not a released design or a ZUFEK test result.

Grade and supplied condition
42CrMo4 bar in the agreed quenched-and-tempered condition. Identify the stock specification, section size and delivery condition on the order.
Finished-part requirement
Specify the required finished mechanical properties and their applicable test basis. Record hardness or local surface requirements separately if the drawing calls for them.
Surface and mating interface
Identify the locating shoulder and thread fit after the specified finish. Include the mating bore and any coating allowance in the review.
Acceptance records
Connect material identity and treatment records to the lot; agree which final-part measurements or mechanical results are required.
Alternative to review, not assume
C45/C45E may enter a different route review; SAE 4140 needs its own governing specification. A similar alloy description is not an approved substitution.

Material selection questions

Does 42CrMo4 automatically mean a class 12.9 screw?

No. The grade describes a steel chemistry; class 12.9 is a finished-fastener mechanical requirement within a defined scope. Heat treatment, section size, geometry and verification must support the ordered requirement.

Can a stock certificate replace finished screw inspection?

It can establish the ordered stock identity and reported stock properties. It does not prove dimensions after treatment, coating thickness, finished-thread conformity or every mechanical property of a custom screw.

Why consider this family?

  • Broad choice of grades and final mechanical conditions
  • Suitable route choices include forming and machining, subject to grade
  • Surface protection can be matched to the environment

Application range

Automotive component brackets, machinery connections, fixture shoulder screws and application-specific clamping.

Selection and process considerations

Steel grade, heat treatment and property class are different specifications. Review corrosion exposure, hydrogen-related process risks where applicable, coating friction and dimensional allowances. Reduced-load geometries need their own assessment.

Include in the RFQ

  • Grade and final property requirement
  • Applicable fastener specification and size
  • Heat-treatment and coating system
  • Functional load case and acceptance tests

GRADE / CONDITION / FINAL REQUIREMENT

10B21 Boron Steel

A boron-alloyed steel grade considered for formed fastener routes when the drawing, final material condition and required properties are defined.

On this material page
Grades and conditionsStrength referenceSelection, processing and acceptanceExample material requestMaterial selection questions

Strength reference

10B21 is a grade designation, not a finished strength class. There is no single tensile strength that applies to every 10B21 screw.

Condition-specific mechanical-property references
Grade / condition / basisTensile strength Rm (MPa)Yield / 0.2% stress (MPa)Scope of the reference
10B21 in the required final conditionSpecify for the orderSpecify for the orderForming, heat treatment and final requirements determine the supplied properties.

Values refer to the stated material or fastener-class basis. They are not a certified property or load rating for every ZUFEK custom geometry. Confirm the applicable specification and test condition for the ordered part.

Compare grades and delivery conditions

A material family is a starting point, not a complete specification. The following options are selection references; supply and suitability require drawing review.

Grade comparison for this material family
Grade or specified conditionWhat distinguishes itWhen to consider itWhat to confirm before ordering
10B21 — forming stockState the wire specification and forming condition.Cold-heading route review for repeat quantities.Wire condition is not the final screw condition; request material identification and agreed forming quality.
10B21 — final heat-treated partState final core properties and the required verification.Parts where the approved route includes heat treatment.Do not assume a strength class or prescribe carburizing from the grade name.
10B21 — case requirements, if specifiedState surface/core requirements separately.Only where the drawing calls for an appropriate hardened surface.Agree hardness, case requirements and inspection method; this is not a separate material grade.

How to narrow the choice

These rows describe different order conditions of one grade, not three interchangeable grades. Choose 10B21 only after the supplier reviews the geometry, required final properties and complete treatment route.

Write an unambiguous material requirement

Include the designation standard, exact grade, product form, delivery condition, final mechanical requirements, surface treatment and acceptance evidence. Similar names across EN, ASTM, SAE, JIS or GB systems are comparison leads, not permission to substitute.

If the grade is not yet decided, send the load or locating function, environment, mating materials, quantity and drawing. Ask for a proposed grade and route with stated assumptions before approving the material.

The listed grades are comparisons for drawing review, not a declaration that every grade, size or treatment is held in stock. Availability, route and ordered evidence are confirmed in the quotation.

Selection, processing and acceptance

Choose the grade and condition together with the job the screw performs. The following checks connect the material shortlist to manufacturing and sample acceptance.

Function and grade choice
10B21 is one grade, not a group of strength levels. A formed flange screw and a case-hardened tapping screw can require different final properties even when the starting grade is the same. State whether the part clamps a joint, forms a thread or provides a wear surface before selecting the treatment route.
Processing and final dimensions
Wire preparation, heading stages, secondary machining and thread forming need to suit the geometry and volume. Decide the heat-treatment sequence with the manufacturer. Carburizing is a route for an agreed case requirement, not an automatic instruction attached to 10B21; through-hardening and case-hardening requirements must not be mixed.
What the sample must demonstrate
Define core hardness, surface hardness and case depth only where applicable, with the method and locations to be checked. Connect these results to the treatment batch and inspect relevant dimensions in the final supplied condition. A surface-hardness reading alone does not establish core toughness or the finished strength class.

Example: 10B21 from heading wire to an accepted flange screw

For repeat quantities, describe the incoming wire and finished screw as two different acceptance stages. A formable starting condition is not the final mechanical requirement.

Grade and supplied condition
10B21 wire under the agreed material specification and cold-heading delivery condition; retain the material and lot identity.
Finished-part requirement
Put the required final fastener properties on the drawing. Where applicable, identify core and case requirements separately rather than prescribing carburizing from the grade name.
Surface and mating interface
Review the bearing face, usable thread and final coating. Define when treatment-sensitive dimensions are accepted.
Acceptance records
Agree material identification, treatment-batch records and final mechanical or hardness checks as applicable to the part.
Alternative to review, not assume
A different wire condition, grade or treatment route can change forming and final properties. Review the complete proposal before sample approval.

Material selection questions

Is there one tensile-strength value for 10B21?

No. Incoming wire, formed parts and heat-treated screws are different conditions. Specify the final properties for the actual part and test basis instead of assigning one strength number to the grade.

Should every 10B21 screw be carburized?

No. Choose the route from the required core and surface behavior. If a hardened case is needed, define its acceptance; otherwise do not add a carburizing requirement solely from the material name.

Why consider this family?

  • Relevant to repeat fastener forming discussions
  • Can be reviewed with the complete heat-treatment route
  • Final requirements can distinguish core properties and surface condition

Application range

Drawing-defined production screws, flange parts and selected high-volume automotive or equipment fastener applications.

Selection and process considerations

Do not prescribe carburizing solely because the drawing says 10B21. State the required final mechanical properties and any case-depth or hardness requirements where relevant. Confirm the actual grade, processing route and material documentation during quotation.

Include in the RFQ

  • Exact grade and material condition
  • Required finished properties
  • Core or case requirements where applicable
  • Treatment records and mechanical acceptance

SUS304 & SUS316 Stainless Steel

Austenitic stainless choices for parts where corrosion exposure, surface condition and the specified fastener strength class need to be considered together.

Turn the material shortlist into an order requirement ↓
On this material page
Grades and conditionsStrength referenceSelection, processing and acceptanceExample material requestMaterial selection questions

Strength reference

A2/A4 groups and classes such as 70 or 80 describe finished stainless fasteners under the applicable specification. SUS304 or SUS316 alone does not establish A2-70 or A4-80 performance.

Condition-specific mechanical-property references
Grade / condition / basisTensile strength Rm (MPa)Yield / 0.2% stress (MPa)Scope of the reference
ISO 3506 class 70 reference700 minimum450 minimumApplicable austenitic fasteners; confirm grade, size and product scope.
ISO 3506 class 80 reference800 minimum600 minimumApplicable austenitic fasteners; verify the ordered class and scope.

Values refer to the stated material or fastener-class basis. They are not a certified property or load rating for every ZUFEK custom geometry. Confirm the applicable specification and test condition for the ordered part.

Compare grades and delivery conditions

A material family is a starting point, not a complete specification. The following options are selection references; supply and suitability require drawing review.

Grade comparison for this material family
Grade or specified conditionWhat distinguishes itWhen to consider itWhat to confirm before ordering
304 / SUS304General-purpose austenitic stainless; specify the governing standard.General equipment and enclosure fasteners in suitable environments.Not corrosion-proof; review exposure, galling and final fastener class.
304L / SUS304LLower-carbon variant of the 304 family.Consider when welding or fabrication-related corrosion requirements call for it.The L suffix does not mean a higher strength class.
316 / SUS316Molybdenum-bearing austenitic stainless.Consider when the exposure assessment calls for improved resistance over 304.Chloride concentration, temperature and crevices still require review.
316L / SUS316LLower-carbon variant of the 316 family.Consider where fabrication or welding requirements justify the lower-carbon grade.Specify grade and final condition rather than assuming every 316 part is 316L.
303Free-machining austenitic grade.Turned parts where machining productivity is important and corrosion requirements permit it.Do not substitute for 304 or 316 without assessing corrosion and fabrication requirements.
17-4PH / UNS S17400Precipitation-hardening stainless, distinct from 304/316.A separate comparison when the required strength and corrosion balance justify it.Order the aging condition, such as H900 or H1150, with the product specification; properties differ by condition.

How to narrow the choice

Start with the exposure and fabrication requirements, then assess manufacturing and assembly. A2/A4 fastener groups are not universal synonyms for a specific JIS or ASTM grade. Order the exact grade plus the applicable finished fastener class; passivation does not upgrade 304 into 316.

Write an unambiguous material requirement

Include the designation standard, exact grade, product form, delivery condition, final mechanical requirements, surface treatment and acceptance evidence. Similar names across EN, ASTM, SAE, JIS or GB systems are comparison leads, not permission to substitute.

If the grade is not yet decided, send the load or locating function, environment, mating materials, quantity and drawing. Ask for a proposed grade and route with stated assumptions before approving the material.

The listed grades are comparisons for drawing review, not a declaration that every grade, size or treatment is held in stock. Availability, route and ordered evidence are confirmed in the quotation.

Selection, processing and acceptance

Choose the grade and condition together with the job the screw performs. The following checks connect the material shortlist to manufacturing and sample acceptance.

Function and grade choice
For general equipment, compare 304 with the actual moisture and cleaning exposure. Consider 316 where its molybdenum-bearing composition suits the corrosion assessment, not simply because the part is outdoors. Use 303 when machining benefits justify its different corrosion and fabrication behavior. Review 17-4PH separately when a precipitation-hardening route is needed.
Processing and final dimensions
Austenitic 304/316 can gain strength through cold work; conventional quench-and-temper treatment does not turn them into high-strength martensitic screws. For 17-4PH, name the aging condition and plan dimensional acceptance after treatment. Passivation is a surface process, not a change from 304 to 316 or a method of assigning class 80.
What the sample must demonstrate
Identify the grade, ordered condition and any applicable finished-fastener class independently. For repeated assembly, review mating materials, lubrication or coating and the tightening method to manage galling. Agree corrosion or surface acceptance for the actual exposure; a material certificate and a salt-spray result answer different questions.

Example: a SUS316 cable feed-through for an outdoor enclosure

Specify the exposure and passage function alongside the grade. Outdoor use alone does not define chloride exposure, cleaning conditions or the mechanical demand on the connection.

Illustrative material request. Drawing-specific limits and acceptance criteria remain to be agreed; this is not a released design or a ZUFEK test result.

Grade and supplied condition
SUS316 bar with the governing material standard and supplied condition stated. Identify whether the drawing actually calls for SUS316 or SUS316L.
Finished-part requirement
Specify any applicable finished fastener class independently of the stock grade. Check the hollow section and mating connection against the actual load.
Surface and mating interface
Define the bore edges, contact with dissimilar metals, cleaning and any passivation. Check usable thread and final passage clearance after processing.
Acceptance records
Request the agreed grade/lot record and final checks. Record the specified surface treatment separately from material identity.
Alternative to review, not assume
303 favors a different machining/corrosion balance; 304 or 316L needs an application review rather than a name-based substitution.

Material selection questions

Is 316L stronger than 316?

The L suffix identifies a lower-carbon variant, not a higher strength level. Compare properties for the same product and condition, and select the low-carbon grade for the fabrication and corrosion requirements that justify it.

Are A2-70 and SUS304 the same specification?

No. A2-70 combines a stainless fastener group with a property class; SUS304 identifies a material grade under its governing specification. State both material identity and finished-fastener requirements where both are needed.

Why consider this family?

  • Useful for corrosion-exposed equipment and accessible exterior hardware
  • Grade and finish can be chosen for the actual medium
  • Commonly discussed for machined and custom-formed screw geometries

Application range

Equipment covers, electronic and optical housings, outdoor security hardware and selected fluid-handling connections.

Selection and process considerations

304 and 316 are not precipitation-hardening grades. Review the actual environment rather than assuming any stainless part is corrosion-proof. Consider thread galling, mating metals, cleaning and passivation. Form and final condition affect the mechanical requirements.

Include in the RFQ

  • 304 or 316 grade requirement
  • Finished fastener class where applicable
  • Exposure medium and mating metals
  • Surface condition, passivation and thread acceptance

Aluminum Alloys

Lightweight metal options for custom threaded parts where the alloy, temper, engagement and surface requirements can be engineered for the application.

On this material page
Grades and conditionsStrength referenceSelection, processing and acceptanceExample material requestMaterial selection questions

Strength reference

The same alloy in a different temper has different properties. The figures below are examples for specified extruded stock, not a finished screw rating.

Condition-specific mechanical-property references
Grade / condition / basisTensile strength Rm (MPa)Yield / 0.2% stress (MPa)Scope of the reference

Values refer to the stated material or fastener-class basis. They are not a certified property or load rating for every ZUFEK custom geometry. Confirm the applicable specification and test condition for the ordered part.

Compare grades and delivery conditions

A material family is a starting point, not a complete specification. The following options are selection references; supply and suitability require drawing review.

Grade comparison for this material family
Grade or specified conditionWhat distinguishes itWhen to consider itWhat to confirm before ordering
6061-T6 / T6511Alloy plus temper and product form must be stated.Lightweight machined adjustment or enclosure components.T6511 is a stock temper designation, not a general finished-screw strength guarantee.

6061 or 6082 in another temperThe alloy number stays the same while condition changes.Forming or fabrication routes that require a different supplied condition.Properties quoted for T6 stock cannot be assigned to unspecified or annealed stock.

How to narrow the choice

Specify alloy, temper and bar or extrusion specification before comparing strength. Review thread engagement, bearing surfaces, anodizing allowance and mating-metal corrosion as separate joint-design questions.

Write an unambiguous material requirement

Include the designation standard, exact grade, product form, delivery condition, final mechanical requirements, surface treatment and acceptance evidence. Similar names across EN, ASTM, SAE, JIS or GB systems are comparison leads, not permission to substitute.

If the grade is not yet decided, send the load or locating function, environment, mating materials, quantity and drawing. Ask for a proposed grade and route with stated assumptions before approving the material.

The listed grades are comparisons for drawing review, not a declaration that every grade, size or treatment is held in stock. Availability, route and ordered evidence are confirmed in the quotation.

Selection, processing and acceptance

Choose the grade and condition together with the job the screw performs. The following checks connect the material shortlist to manufacturing and sample acceptance.

Function and grade choice
6061 and 6082 are useful starting comparisons for lightweight machined parts. Consider 7075 only when its grade-specific strength and environmental trade-offs justify it. A higher tensile value does not solve limited engagement in a soft mating thread, concentrated bearing pressure or wear from repeated adjustment.
Processing and final dimensions
T6 identifies a heat-treatment state; T6511 additionally identifies stretching-related stress relief for applicable extrusions. They are not generic labels for all bar forms. Review anodizing thickness, masking and the final thread or shoulder fit. A later thermal operation or welding can change the condition on which the stock property data were based.
What the sample must demonstrate
Specify the actual alloy, temper, product form and section size. Check the final usable thread, bearing face and fitted dimensions after the agreed finish. For an adjuster, trial the travel and locking arrangement with the real mating component; agree any assembly test separately from the stock tensile certificate.

Example: a 6061-T6511 machined adjustment screw

For a lightweight adjuster, carry the stock temper into the specification, then evaluate the thread and bearing interface in the finished assembly.

Illustrative material request. Drawing-specific limits and acceptance criteria remain to be agreed; this is not a released design or a ZUFEK test result.

Grade and supplied condition
6061-T6511 extruded bar under the agreed product specification. Record the stock size and condition used for the reference properties.
Finished-part requirement
Distinguish stock tensile data from finished-thread acceptance. Identify engagement, adjustment duty and any required assembly verification.
Surface and mating interface
Define anodizing or another specified finish, the affected dimensions and the mating material. Check the usable thread and fit in the final supplied condition.
Acceptance records
Retain grade/temper and lot identification; agree dimensional results after finishing and any specified treatment records.
Alternative to review, not assume
6082 or another temper requires comparison on the same product and condition basis. Do not transfer a T6 reference value to unspecified stock.

Material selection questions

Can 7075 replace 6061 without changing the drawing?

Treat it as a material change. Compare the required temper, corrosion exposure, machining and finishing route, mating metal and final acceptance. A higher strength reference alone does not authorize the substitution.

Does anodizing increase the strength class of an aluminum screw?

Anodizing changes the surface and can affect dimensions, wear and friction. It does not assign a finished-fastener strength class or replace the specified alloy and temper.

Why consider this family?

  • Lower component mass than an equivalent-volume steel part
  • Machined geometry can combine steps, bores and adjustment features
  • Surface finish and alloy temper can be reviewed together

Application range

Lightweight electronic assemblies, optical adjustment hardware, equipment covers and custom low-mass fixture components.

Selection and process considerations

Specify alloy and temper. Review thread stripping and engagement in the real joint, contact with dissimilar metals, wear, finishing allowance and assembly torque. Stock tensile properties do not by themselves establish the load capacity of a threaded component.

Include in the RFQ

  • Alloy, temper and stock form
  • Mating thread and engagement
  • Surface finish or anodizing requirement
  • Joint load and assembly conditions
